Sports.title: Gianni Infantino ‘has lost Uefa’s confidence’ after Fifa chief scraps World Cup sell-off plan
Sports.content:
Uefa has warned Gianni Infantino that his style of leadership cannot continue in demanding a thorough and fundamental review of Fifa’s governance.

In a strongly worded statement that referred to “secret schemes”, “shabby backroom deals” and “faceless individuals”, the Uefa leadership made clear it wants change at the top of Fifa, despite the world governing body’s overnight U-turn in abandoning Infantino’s plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup and other competitions.

While stopping short of calling for Infantino to resign, Uefa’s leadership is understood to be determined that he should not be permitted to survive a crisis of his own making, a view that is shared by many of the biggest football governing bodies across the world. Leading European officials are already understood to have begun the process of identifying a candidate to stand against Infantino in next year’s Fifa presidential election, which will continue over the next few days.

Uefa’s statement made clear that under the leadership of president Aleksander Ceferin, who succeeded in getting all 55 member associations to support a World Cup boycott last Thursday, it will continue to push for change.

“We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game,” the statement read. “We must identify those responsible and hold them to account.

“It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, Uefa will work with its associations and in close cooperation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again. That review should be thorough and fundamental. No option should be off the table. The current Fifa leadership has not only lost Uefa’s confidence, but also that of many other members of the football family.”

Uefa went on to criticise Infantino directly, saying he has failed to deliver on pledges he made to be transparent and accountable before he was first elected president in 2016.

View image in fullscreen Aleksander Ceferin and Gianni Infantino, pictured together in 2024. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA

The Football Association backed Uefa and, in a statement, said: “We fully support Uefa’s position. It is time for a full and robust review of Fifa’s leadership and governance to ensure that the global game is run transparently, for the benefit of all 211 member nations and with the long-term stewardship of football at its heart!”

Elsewhere in Europe, the Dutch FA said the withdrawal of Infantino’s proposal was not the end of the issue, adding: “The matter is ⁠not settled for the KNVB. The way this process has unfolded has led to a fundamental breach of trust in the leadership of Fifa president Gianni Infantino. The KNVB no longer has ⁠confidence in his leadership.“

Infantino had been expected to be re-elected unopposed for a third full term at next March’s Fifa Congress in Rabat, but while he is determined to stay on the 56-year-old could now face a challenger. While he has already secured more than 200 letters of support from member associations endorsing his re-election campaign they can be withdrawn, and the deadline for other candidates to announce an intention to stand is not until 18 November.

The Paris Saint-Germain president Nasser Al-Khelaifi is favoured by many in Europe, but appears reluctant to stand and is also chair of powerful lobby group, European Football Clubs. Other potential candidates include Victor Montagliani, the Canadian who is the president of North American confederation Concacaf, and the Asian Football Confederation president Salman al-Khalifa, who lost narrowly to Infantino in the 2016 Fifa election.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Uefa’s statement used Infantino’s own words from his initial election campaign 10 years ago against him. “When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of Fifa’s Member Associations to elect him as their president in 2016, he said, ‘Of course we have to be transparent. I have been this in the last 15 years of my life in Uefa. You will have to play a part every day in the life of Fifa,’ before telling the assembled stakeholders, ‘The money of Fifa is your money. It’s not the money of the Fifa president. It’s your money. You are the national associations, and the money of Fifa has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else.’ On both these promises, he has failed to deliver. The shabby, back room, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through were anything but transparent. And with reserves standing at over $5bn, he has also failed to use associations’ money for the benefit of the game.”

Uefa also called for an immediate overhaul of Fifa’s system of financial distribution, the Fifa Forward programme in which all 211 member associations receive the same central payment from Fifa over each four-year cycle. Infantino had claimed that selling 20% of a new commercial company – Fifa Forward Enterprise – to private investors would enable them to increase the Fifa Forward payments from $8m over the next four-year cycle to $20m, as well as a one-off $20m bonus for signing up to the scheme.

View image in fullscreen The Fifa logo in front of its headquarters in Zurich, Switzerland. Gianni Infantino’s senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro and chief operating officer Kevin Lamour opposed his plan. Photograph: Arnd Wiegmann/Reuters

Handing out millions of dollars to tiny nations has been widely criticised as a system of patronage designed to keep Infantino in office, while the $20m bonus on offer for associations who signed up by a deadline of 19 September was condemned.

“Uefa will begin work immediately with partners and stakeholders all over the world and right across the game to propose a new way of distributing resources through the existing Fifa Forward programme,” its statement continued. “We must start to use some of that money that is sat idle in Fifa’s bank account to deliver the kick start that the grassroots and the wider game need in each of the 211 countries of Fifa. But we don’t need to sell off the family silver to pay for it.

“This is a victory for the whole game. But it must not be the end of the story. The proposal has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in Fifa has only just begun.”

Sports.title: Women’s football continues to be used as a pawn in Gianni Infantino’s Fifa tenure | Suzanne Wrack
Sports.content:
Despite not having been deemed worthy of more than a single mention in Fifa’s 25-page sales deck to its 211 member associations on its doomed proposal to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors, now very expensive waste paper, it was women’s football that had found itself on the frontline in the fight for the “soul of football”.

Uefa’s statement that European national teams would not “participate in any Fifa competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that Fifa will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership”, was a bold, necessary and effective declaration of war against the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino.

However, with the Under-20 Women’s World Cup being held in Poland next month; the Under-17 Women’s World Cup and Uefa’s qualifying playoffs for the senior tournament both beginning in October; and the big one, the Women’s World Cup itself, taking place in Brazil next summer, women’s tournaments would have been the first test cases had a boycott gone ahead.

There was no further detail on the FA’s plans for England’s two-legged World Cup playoff against Greece, but Uefa’s call for a boycott would have had an impact on the women’s game in September.

A boycott of the Women’s World Cup would have been catastrophic and yet that was the likely consequence of Infantino’s deadline. The 2023 Women’s World Cup was the first to break even after generating more than $570m (£424m) in revenue and Fifa said in May 2025 it is targeting $1bn in revenue from the 2027 edition.

The women’s game is so desperately reliant on international competition for accelerating its growth that the knock-on impact of having no World Cup would have set progress back far more than four years.

However, Uefa was not wrong in its stance and the subsequent collapse of Infantino’s masterplan after the almighty fallout from demonstrates as much. It was not European football’s governing body that engineered the timeframe that put women’s football on the frontline and it was correct not to exclude women’s football, or youth football, from its arsenal in the fight back against Infantino’s attempt to steamroller through his plans.

View image in fullscreen England’s dream of avenging their World Cup final defeat in 2023 was thrown into doubt by Gianni Infantino’s proposals. Photograph: Zac Goodwin/PA

The blame for the threat posed by a boycott on women’s football lay squarely at the feet of Gianni “I have four daughters” Infantino, who was praised in February by Jill Ellis, Fifa’s chief football officer and twice a World Cup-winning coach, for his “commitment to accelerating the women’s game and increasing women’s influence in shaping its future” and under whose leadership “investment has moved from rhetoric to action”.

To an extent Ellis is right – Infantino is the Fifa president who has done the most for the women’s game. But when his predecessor is Sepp Blatter, a man who said in 2004 that “tighter shorts” was the way to get more people watching the women’s game, the bar is staggeringly low.

Yes, under Infantino Fifa has invested more in the women’s game than ever before, but it has been a pawn in his tenure: initially useful for showing just how progressive and in tune with modern society he and Fifa are, and now useful because it presents an opportunity for medium- to long-term financial gain as one of the fastest growing and least‑tapped areas of the game.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Step behind the rhetoric and handouts and Infantino’s real attitude to the women’s game is evident. In 2023 Sky News reported the Fifa president had left the Women’s World Cup for Tahiti after less than a week, before returning later in the tournament. By contrast, he went to at least some part of every one of the 64 games of the 2022 men’s World Cup and at times appeared at two a day during the latest men’s edition despite the huge environmental impact of using a private jet.

View image in fullscreen The 2027 Women’s World Cup in Brazil starts in less than 11 months. Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/Reuters

Perhaps Infantino waited until the beginning of a new four-year men’s World Cup cycle to try to limit the impact of any backlash on the showpiece event, but in doing so he added to the pile of evidence demonstrative of real attitude towards women’s football, with women’s edition of the tournament on the imminent horizon.

It would have been oddly fitting, then, if the women’s game had become the sun that melted his Icarus wings. Luckily, women’s football didn’t have to pay that costly price. However, this episode must act as a warning, both to those who care about the development of the women’s game and its future and those who care about the future of the men’s game.

The reality is that the European Super League debacle and this latest and most blatant of attempts to hand the wealth of football to private finance vultures show that private finance will keep coming back as they search for ways to get a piece of the pie.

Sports.title: Have you ever switched allegiance as a football fan? You are not alone | Luke McLaughlin
Sports.content:
“I was fanatically pro-German when the Germans were here to protect us against the Americans, and now that Americans are here to protect us against the Germans, I am fanatically pro-American … you and your country will have no more loyal partisan in Italy than me – but only as long as you remain in Italy.”

This passage from Joseph Heller’s Catch-22 – as an old Italian man explains the logic behind his fickle wartime expedience to a naive American soldier – plays with the question of what constitutes true strength. Universally perceived as weak, Italy are in fact the strongest nation in the second world war, according to the old man. And that, sort of, explains my feelings on football fandom.

My dad was passionate about cricket and chess. But I was a football-mad kid, and he dutifully escorted my brother and I to watch West Ham v Nottingham Forest at Upton Park in November 1987. Dad naturally knew about Brian Clough and correctly predicted it would be an entertaining game: the hosts won 3-2.

After that ridiculously exciting day as a 10-year-old, and despite living in south London, I became a Forest supporter, despite photos existing of me in Everton and Tottenham kits earlier in childhood. My mid-1980s decision to support Everton, for clarity, had been pure, unadulterated glory-hunting. Why I then decided to switch to Tottenham, I don’t recall, but it may have had something to do with Paul Gascoigne’s unique ability.

Geographically I should have supported Crystal Palace or Millwall given I was brought up between their grounds: I vividly remember visiting the Den with a Swindon-supporting schoolmate during the era of Terry Hurlock.

As a cricket fan, I have stuck with Middlesex since childhood, but there was never any familial impetus to support a football club. My brother became an Arsenal fan and when I was old enough to regularly attend games alone I started following Forest around London, including a draw at the Den in 1993-94 marred by post-match violence after a Stan Collymore equaliser ended Millwall’s playoff hopes.

When Forest sank into the doldrums after the magical mid-90s, I started to pay less attention to them in classic fairweather-fan fashion. Recently, when living in Somerset, I dabbled with being a Yeovil supporter. Now back living in London I am a regular patron at the Den and have begun to follow Millwall’s results more than Forest’s.

It’s not unusual to support an overseas club either, and after a formative experience watching Napoli lose to Chelsea in 2012 a passion for the Italian club emerged. I’ve visited Naples several times, made good friends there and seen a few games. The most memorable trip was in May 2023 when the Serie A title was sealed under Luciano Spalletti. I didn’t have a ticket but ultimately didn’t need one: the entire city was electrified by their (our) third scudetto.

View image in fullscreen ‘As a teenage follower of Forest, I felt my personal fortunes were linked to the club’s.’ Bayern Munich’s Jürgen Klinsmann takes on Steve Chettle in 1996. Photograph: Lee Beskeen/Action

For some people switching, or even mixing, football allegiances remains taboo. Devoted supporters of a single club may regard my experience as a sign of weakness, or at least exceptional fickleness. But “fan” is short for “fanatic”, and I am no longer convinced so much emotional energy should be invested in supporting any club. Why, after all, would I associate my happiness and sense of fulfilment with something I can’t control? Was the obvious and sustained misery of Arsenal fans as they edged nervously to the Premier League title worth the payoff? Perhaps it was, but there is clearly something unhealthy in that level of obsession.

It is possible, after all, to be too emotionally invested in a certain outcome for your own wellbeing. As an avid teenage follower of Forest, I felt my personal fortunes were linked to the club’s. I regarded one particularly inept late-90s defeat by Wimbledon as a personal tragedy that raised serious questions about my future happiness. I still love football – I am just more ambivalent to its outcomes.

Not only is it acceptable to switch allegiance, it actually makes more sense to base your support on what’s going on in your life at the time. If professional athletes can represent more than one country, let alone several clubs, why shouldn’t fans switch teams?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The disparity between mercenary players and loyal fans grows ever bigger and more grotesque. The players earn obscene amounts of money, and wield a disproportionate amount of power, but often show zero loyalty to a club and its fans when a better offer appears. How can any of this make sense for the lifelong supporter?

And being a diehard fan can be a compromising position in so many ways, frequently leading to defending the indefensible, from unethical petro-state sportwashing and financial doping to obvious on-field foul play and even spying. If you are a glory-hunting Manchester City devotee with a hidden Manchester United-supporting past, or have ever done a football-supporting switcheroo of any kind, do not be ashamed. There is help available. There are people who understand.

Since becoming a regular attendee at Millwall, I’ve enjoyed watching matches with one of my oldest friends and his son. A tight, noisy, old-fashioned ground, no video assistant referee, close to home … have I finally become a real fan?

As long as I live in London I will enjoy following Millwall … with Forest and Napoli thrown in. Not forgetting Dulwich Hamlet. Should I ever return to Somerset, though, I’ll be Yeovil till I die.

Sports.title: Marketing stunt or ‘extraordinary’ transfer? Ravenna fans ride wave of the Ronaldinho Effect
Sports.content:
On a scorching summer afternoon in Ravenna, a city far better known for its fifth-century Byzantine mosaics and Dante’s tomb than for footballing glory, eyes are peeled in the historic centre for one of world football’s most recognisable figures – a man who featured in the World Cup final half-time show alongside Madonna and Ronaldo: Ronaldo de Assis Moreira, better known as Ronaldinho.

“We haven’t seen him yet,” four Ravenna supporters sitting at a cafe say with dry irony as they flip through La Gazzetta dello Sport, Italy’s famous pink sports daily. They are undeniably sceptical, viewing the signing as a purely commercial operation, yet deep down they still harbour the dream of seeing the 2005 Ballon d’Or and 2002 World Cup winner wear their yellow and red shirt.

It is a small, surreal glimpse into the whirlwind that has engulfed this quiet corner of Emilia-Romagna, thanks to the business instinct of Ignazio Cipriani. Heir to the Venetian hospitality dynasty behind the renowned Harry’s Bar, Cipriani took over the club in 2024 when they were in Serie D, the fourth tier of Italian football. A native of Ravenna, he is the grandson of Raul Gardini, the Italian chemicals tycoon and sailor who steered Il Moro di Venezia to the 1992 America’s Cup final.

In his first year as president, Cipriani oversaw victory in the Serie D Cup and promotion to the professional ranks of Serie C. But that is merely the first step in a long ascent, he says: “It’s not a provocation. Serie A is the goal I declared from day one because I intend to reach it. And the Champions League remains the ultimate horizon we want to walk towards, step by step. I made this statement because I like working with my back against the wall: when you have no way out, you are forced to find solutions instead of excuses. I prefer to remove every alibi from the beginning.”

And this summer, Cipriani pulled off a surprise move – so surprising that anyone reading the headlines assumed it was a prank: bringing the 46-year-old Ronaldinho back as a player.

View image in fullscreen Ronaldinho holds up a Ravenna top with Ignazio Cipriani, the club president, after the surprise move was announced in Miami in June. Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/AP

“We met through Lorenzo Tonetti and Ariedo Braida,” Cipriani says, “two people who worked for over 20 years at AC Milan and had Ronaldinho as a player. The idea of involving him was a dream I cultivated as soon as I bought the club. Thanks to Lorenzo and Ariedo, we met, started talking, and a genuine friendship grew. From that relationship came many ideas for the club’s growth. And to the question everyone is asking, I am happy to answer: Ronaldinho will wear the Ravenna shirt as a player, and he will try – maybe scoring the last goal of his career with us!”

Meanwhile, a dedicated website has already put a special-edition shirt on sale featuring the “R10” logo – the Brazilian’s personal brand – which sold out within a few hours. It represents a striking collision of high-end global branding, small-town football, and brilliantly executed marketing stunt.

“If someone had told me three years ago that Ronaldinho was coming to Ravenna, I would have sent them straight to the psychiatric ward,” says Fabio laughing, a lifelong supporter. “The night the news broke, international headlines everywhere read ‘Ronaldinho to Ravenna’. It was an extraordinary operation.”

Ravenna is no footballing giant. Plagued by bankruptcies in 2001 and 2012, the club has spent decades bouncing around the lower tiers, with seven seasons in Serie B the highest point. Historically a volleyball stronghold, the football scene was accustomed to modest budgets and regional rivalries.

View image in fullscreen Ronaldinho will be aiming to wow the crowds at Ravenna’s Stadio Bruno Benelli this season. Photograph: Roberto Salomone/The Guardian

“Ronaldinho is a unique icon,” Cipriani says. “His way of playing made my generation fall in love with the game. We want him today to make the next generation of fans, in Italy and around the world, fall in love with Ravenna . It’s not just a visibility stunt; it’s about building a bridge between different eras of football and growing a truly global fanbase around it.”

To support this ambitious sporting and industrial project, the club is working with the municipality to renovate the Stadio Bruno Benelli, increasing its capacity beyond 6,300. But the president’s ultimate dream is a new multi-purpose venue open seven days a week, featuring retail spaces, concert facilities, and an integrated Hotel Cipriani linked to the city’s international tourism expansion.

For Ravenna’s mayor, Alessandro Barattoni, the arrival of a world-famous figure fits neatly into a broader strategy to promote the city globally. In recent years, Ravenna has been expanding its international reach beyond traditional beach tourism and commercial ports. The city is enjoying renewed ties with the Anglo-Saxon world, highlighted by a recent visit from the British royal family and the opening of the Lord Byron Museum.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“Ronaldinho brings a whole new level of global fame,” Barattoni says. “When the news broke, my phone exploded with messages from former schoolmates. For younger kids today, he might be someone to discover on YouTube, but the fascination remains intact.” With a smile, the mayor adds that, schedule permitting, he would be delighted to personally guide Ronaldinho on a tour of the city’s cultural heritage.

However, Barattoni is quick to clarify the institution’s role: “Our common ground with the club is internationalisation: bringing Ravenna’s image to the world. Ronaldinho has been a global ambassador for countless brands. There is an overarching project that can bring great visibility to the team and allow the city to showcase its initiatives beyond standard routes.” He adds: “Even before Ronaldinho’s arrival, the club did a fantastic job engaging younger generations. The average age in the stands is lower, more vibrant, and more engaged than ever before. A genuine sense of community is forming.”

View image in fullscreen Alessandro Barattoni, the mayor of Ravenna, is confident the Ronaldinho transfer will be positive for the Italian city. Photograph: Roberto Salomone/The Guardian

Yet, fears of a hyper-commercialised image linger among traditional supporters. In the Curva Mero, such marketing moves are approached with caution. “There is a certain reluctance among some factions,” Fabio admits. “Modern football pushes values that many don’t share: rising ticket prices, losing accessibility for lower-income families. As a result, visibility and marketing stunts risk being viewed sideways.”

Cipriani demonstrates an acute awareness of these dynamics: “Without roots, no global project makes sense,” the president says. “Ravenna is not a brand we are building from scratch; it’s a history and an identity that existed before us. Tradition isn’t a brake on ambition: it’s the foundation. A club without its people is worth nothing.”

“I’m 50 years old and I’ve been coming to the stadium since my school days,” says Giovanni, another fan. “I’m rediscovering the enthusiasm of the past. If it takes an icon like Ronaldinho and a local entrepreneur to make us dream of Serie A, then so be it. The important thing is never to forget the people in the stands.”

Riding the wave of the “Ronaldinho Effect”, the season-ticket campaign has just launched with a target of selling 2,800. Ticket prices have risen by an average of about 12%, with variations across different stadium sections.

For now, Ravenna is soaking up a dizzying, galvanising atmosphere. On the pitch, the club is assembling a squad to win the league; off it, the city awaits 20 August, when Ronaldinho is expected to appear during a three-day summer festival in nearby Marina di Ravenna, organised in signature Cipriani style.

Sports.title: Rangers held by Dundee United to kick off McInnes era and Scottish Premiership
Sports.content:
Thelo Aasgaard earned Derek McInnes his first point as Rangers manager as they fought back for a 1-1 draw against Dundee United.

Lachlan Rose struck the first goal of the Premiership season to give United a half-time lead at Tannadice.

Rangers lacked control in possession in the opening period but they looked more threatening after the break and Aasgaard finished brilliantly in the 56th minute. They could not build on the equaliser, though, as United soon stemmed the tide of pressure.

View image in fullscreen Dundee United’s Lachlan Rose celebrates after opening the scoring. Photograph: Russell Cheyne/Reuters

Jesse Randall should have won the game for the home side with eight minutes left when substitute Daniel Bennie’s swerving pass put the New Zealand international clean through on goal. However, the winger totally lacked conviction as he dinked a shot straight into goalkeeper Ivor Pandur’s hands.

McInnes named Youssef Chermiti on the bench in his first team selection with Ryan Naderi handed a role on the right of Rangers’ attack, and Pandur, Ben Godfrey, Cammy Devlin and Lawrence Shankland making their debuts.

There were only two Scots in the two starting lineups but both led their teams, former Falkirk midfielder Dylan Tait wearing the armband for United and Shankland the new Rangers captain.

The former Hearts striker was the first to threaten with a flick that drew a reaction stop from Jack Walton, but the home goalkeeper’s only other first-half save came from a Naderi header which looked like it was slightly off target. Rose and Zac Sapsford got in behind for the home side but could not get shots on target and the Rangers defence was busy on other occasions as United worked the ball into the box.

View image in fullscreen Derek McInnes began his time at Rangers with a hard-fought 1-1 draw at Dundee United on the opening day of the season. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Dujon Sterling and Mohamed Diomande were off target from outside the box for Rangers, before the hosts made the breakthrough in the 38th minute. Rangers centre-back Emmanuel Fernandez was out of position as Sapsford dummied Randall’s low cross and Rose watched in delight as his left-foot effort spun off the post and over the line.

Chermiti and Dan Neil came on for Naderi and Djeidi Gassama as McInnes tried to affect the game at half-time and his side immediately looked more threatening.

Quick Guide Bellingham watches Birmingham beat Barça in friendly Show Jude Bellingham returned to St Andrew's as a spectator to see Birmingham City beat Barcelona on penalties in a pre-season friendly. The England and Real Madrid midfielder (pictured) emerged from Birmingham's academy, making his first-team debut at 16 years old before joining Borussia Dortmund in 2020. August Priske put Birmingham ahead in the 31st minute, but teenage Barça striker Hamza Abdelkarim levelled from the penalty spot before half-time. Abdelkarim struck again on the hour, reacting fastest after Roony Bardghji's shot was saved. Jhon Solis responded for the hosts, volleying home in the 68th minute. The game ended 2-2 after 90 minutes, with Birmingham keeper James Beadle saving twice and 17-year-old Barcelona defender Jordi hitting the crossbar. The shootout ended 3-2 to Birmingham as the hosts enjoyed a memorable victory over an admittedly inexperienced Barcelona line-up. Guardian sport Photograph: Nigel French/PA Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Aasgaard forced an excellent diving save from Walton before the Norway international levelled moments later. Shankland’s physical presence caused problems as United were made to defend another high ball and Aasgaard took an excellent touch to take out Joshua Rawlins before firing a left-foot strike into the top corner from 16 yards.

Rangers could not keep up the momentum, and Randall squandered a glorious chance to mark his league debut with a famous winner. Chermiti almost made the home side pay but Walton stopped the striker’s effort with his feet before home substitute Idjessi Metsoko delivered a weak effort straight at Pandur from a decent opportunity.

Sports.title: Arsenal’s title defence: keeping tired players fit and the Vinícius question
Sports.content:
After beating MK Dons 3-0 in a training-ground friendly last weekend, Arsenal truly begin their pre-season programme against Girona on Saturday evening. It marks a return to action for the Premier League champions, who will want to show their success last season was not a one-off.

Retaining the English title is incredibly difficult if you are not Manchester City. No other club has done it since Manchester United won three in succession from 2007 to 2009. Chelsea have done it once, Liverpool have not managed it for more than 40 years, and it is the best part of a century since Arsenal retained the crown. Mikel Arteta faces a sizeable challenge.

Reaching a second successive Champions League final will not be simple either. Manchester City in 2021-22 are the only one of England’s previous five finalists who made it as far as the semi-finals the next season. With the Premier League stronger than ever, competing on two fronts has never been tougher. Transfer business may improve Arsenal’s chances, though their spending has been modest to this point. More than half of the £79m spent was on making Piero Hincapié’s loan permanent.

Elsewhere Arsenal have replaced Leandro Trossard with Christos Tzolis, a Greek winger, from Club Brugge. Seven years younger than the Belgian, his arrival is a logical move in future-proofing the squad. However, the left side of Arsenal’s attack would be elevated to truly elite level if they could secure reported target Vinícius Júnior. The on-field argument speaks for itself. Vinícius made 92 carries of at least five metres that ended with him either taking a shot (49) or creating a chance (43) last season, the most of anyone in Europe’s top five leagues. Open-play threat, for a side that has often relied on set pieces, would be considerably increased.

Those holding the purse strings at Arsenal may have pause for thought. Capology’s wage data estimates that Vinícius is the joint-third highest paid player in Europe’s top five leagues, earning in excess of £100,000 a week more than anyone at his potential new club. Would Arsenal be willing to rewrite their wage structure? They should expect calls from the agents of their current players if they are. In this sense, Bradley Barcola, with whom they have also been linked, makes a more plausible target. The issue there would be competition from Liverpool, who are in far greater need of wingers.

This is the test facing Andrea Berta, Arsenal’s sporting director. Improving a squad that is already one of the best around is not easy. When Berta’s arrived last year, the club’s primary targets were said to be Alexander Isak and Benjamin Sesko, both of whom joined rivals instead. The pool of players who could add something significant to Arteta’s options is drying up.

Keeping existing players fit may be more beneficial than enhancing the squad. Arsenal did well to win the league given only a handful of clubs had players that missed more games. Kai Havertz was reportedly their top earner before Bukayo Saka signed a contract extension in February, but he only started seven league games. The captain, Martin Ødegaard, was also unavailable for spells, meaning he and Saka started only 10 Premier League matches together in 2025-26. One of them coincided with the only game for which Declan Rice was injured (the 4-1 home win over Aston Villa), another (another home win, 2-1 against Brighton) when he started at right-back.

View image in fullscreen Mikel Arteta indulges in a bit of training-ground banter with first-team coach Miguel Molina in Girona. Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/Getty Images

This meant Arteta was rarely able to give key men a breather. Arsenal have five of the Premier League’s top 20 players for club minutes in all competitions since the start of last season. Granted, the goalkeeper David Raya is one of them. But their outfield players with more than 4,200 minutes were Rice (4,456 minutes, the 11th most for a Premier League club), Martín Zubimendi (4,298, 15th), William Saliba (4,254, 17th) and Gabriel Magalhães (4,210, 19th), all vital components of the side’s spine.

Saliba also played 795 minutes for France, pushing him past 5,000 minutes before his World Cup was prematurely ended by a back injury that looks likely to sideline him for some time. It is remarkable Rice was able to play 1,026 minutes for England on top of his Arsenal commitments, not least as he has managed nerve pain in a hamstring throughout 2026.

This workload clearly impacted his ability to contribute at his best for Thomas Tuchel this summer, and that will be a concern for Arteta. With Viktor Gyökeres also clocking up plenty of playing time for Sweden, Arsenal have six players with at least 4,400 minutes for club and country since the start of last August.

This may have been a factor in Arsenal opting for a relatively low-key pre-season. They visited Asia last summer, but the trip to Catalonia to play Girona is the furthest they will travel this year. Arsenal also have games in Dublin (against Real Betis) and Cardiff (the Community Shield against City) sandwiching home friendlies against Borussia Dortmund and Como.

With players still recovering from their World Cup exertions, it may be some time before we see the true Arsenal. A combination of fatigue, injuries and potential squad additions means the process could take far longer than would be ideal.

Sports.title: Inter make new approach to Liverpool for Curtis Jones with £30m offer likely
Sports.content:
Inter have made another approach for Curtis Jones and are willing to raise their offer for the Liverpool midfielder to €35m (£30m). The Italian champions had a €25m bid for the 25-year-old rejected in June by Liverpool, who value their homegrown player at closer to €40m.

The England and Real Madrid midfielder (pictured) emerged from Birmingham's academy, making his first-team debut at 16 years old before joining Borussia Dortmund in 2020. August Priske put Birmingham ahead in the 31st minute, but teenage Barça striker Hamza Abdelkarim levelled from the penalty spot before half-time. Abdelkarim struck again on the hour, reacting fastest after Roony Bardghji's shot was saved. Jhon Solis responded for the hosts, volleying home in the 68th minute. The game ended 2-2 after 90 minutes, with Birmingham keeper James Beadle saving twice and 17-year-old Barcelona defender Jordi hitting the crossbar. The shootout ended 3-2 to Birmingham as the hosts enjoyed a memorable victory over an admittedly inexperienced Barcelona line-up. Guardian sport Photograph: Nigel French/PA Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Intermediaries representing Inter have made fresh contact with Liverpool this week and outlined their willingness to go to €35m for a player who has only one year remaining on his contract at Anfield. Whether Liverpool accept that sum is doubtful, but a deal for Jones to leave his boyhood club does appear to be edging closer.

Jones has been unable to establish himself as a regular starter at Liverpool and cut a frustrated figure at times last season under Arne Slot. He was also involved in a row with Dominik Szoboszlai after Wednesday’s win over Wrexham in New York, seemingly over not being handed the captain’s armband when Szoboszlai was substituted during the second half of the friendly.
