World.title: The split in Poland’s opposition could help them unseat Tusk’s government [Opinion]
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles If Mateusz Morawiecki cuts his final ties with PiS and forms a new party, it may help broaden the opposition’s appeal by offering voters a more moderate, centre-right option. While the strings have not yet been fully cut, Poland’s main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), is splitting in two. A group of 40 MPs led by former Prime Minister (and PiS deputy leader) Mateusz Morawiecki have now formed a separate parliamentary caucus of their own, after last week refusing to sign a pledge of loyalty and quit the association they had formed – as had been demanded by PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński. Former Polish PM @MorawieckiM says 41 lawmakers aligned with him will form their own parliamentary caucus, deepening a split in conservative opposition party @pisorgpl. The proposed group would become the third-largest bloc in Poland's Sejmhttps://t.co/coOdpS7pia — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 The move means that Morawiecki’s caucus, known as Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), is now the third largest in parliament, while PiS, which is down to 147 MPs, has lost its status as the biggest. For now, most of Morawiecki’s followers officially remain members of the PiS party, a situation that will only change if they either resign or are thrown out following a disciplinary process that could take weeks. But unless either or both sides make major concessions, it seems only a matter of time before Development Plus becomes a separate party. A lot of international reporting has suggested that these developments will harm Poland’s right-wing opposition and boost the re-election chances of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s more liberal coalition at next year’s parliamentary elections. In fact, PiS’s split could well help the opposition win a majority. Over the last year, PiS has found itself in an increasingly difficult position. Its support in the polls has fallen below 25%, the party’s lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, combined support for two far-right opposition groups – Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) – has risen to over 20%, threatening PiS’s longstanding dominance on the right. In response, Kaczyński has pushed his party in a more rightward direction, picking a hardline figure, Przemysław Czarnek, as PiS’s prime ministerial candidate in March. That signalled that PiS was aiming to compete head to head with the far right on many issues, taking tougher positions on Ukraine, the EU, migration and climate policy. In many cases, that meant disowning the legacy of the PiS government led by Morawiecki from 2017 to 2023. It also meant that the party was ceding the centre ground, something Morawiecki, who represents the more moderate, technocratic side of PiS, was particularly concerned about (alongside his own waning influence). When in power, PiS launched a revolution in Poland's energy transition. But now, in opposition, it has disowned those achievements and returned to an emphasis on coal. This could be a missed opportunity to win back centrist voters, writes @OrzelBartlomiej https://t.co/8cGvubn7N2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026 Should Morawiecki now, as expected, launch his own centre-right party, focused on economic development, it would appeal to moderate conservatives who are opposed to the Tusk government but put off by the far right and PiS’s own hardline turn. Inevitably, some of the support for Development Plus would come at the expense of PiS – but not all of it, and possibly not even most of it. An example of something similar happening can be seen elsewhere among the opposition. Until last year, KKP was part of Confederation. However, its leader, Grzegorz Braun, was expelled after announcing a run for the presidency against Confederation’s official candidate, Sławomir Mentzen. In June 2025, KKP formed its own parliamentary caucus. Since then, support for Confederation has remained stable at around 13-14%, while KKP has risen to over 9% in the polls. So, by splitting, the two groups actually increased the size of their potential electorate, with KKP successfully appealing to an even more radical pool of voters than Confederation. It is possible that Morawiecki could do the same in the opposite direction – his new party winning over moderate conservatives while PiS continues to appeal to its most loyal supporters as well as competing with the far right. There certainly seems to be fertile ground for such a party. Regular polling by the state research agency CBOS shows that the proportion of Poles with a negative view of Tusk’s government rose to its joint-highest level this month, at 48%, while only 29% have a positive view. The last time that positive views outnumbered negative ones was in February 2024, the second full month of the current ruling coalition’s time in power. Among those who voted for Tusk and his allies in 2023, dissatisfaction is strongest among moderate conservatives. Both Tusk’s centrist KO and one of his coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), are polling only slightly below the proportion of votes they received in that year (30.7% and 8.6%, respectively). However, the most conservative part of the coalition, the centre-right Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance, has fallen from 14.4% of the vote in 2023 to only around 4-5% today for the two parties that constituted it, Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) and the Polish People’s Party (PSL) (which last year decided to go their separate ways). An IBRiS poll for Polsat News in April this year found that, whereas 84% of KO voters and 57.1% of Left voters have a positive view of Tusk’s government, that figure falls to 42.5% for Third Way voters, a majority of whom (51.6%) have a negative opinion. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 Moderate conservatives’ disillusionment with the government, combined with PiS’s shift away from the centre ground, gives a clear opportunity for Morawiecki. And Tusk’s coalition itself showed in 2023 the advantages for the opposition in offering a broader set of options. While some – in KO in particular – had pushed for centrist and left-wing parties to stand jointly on a single list at that year’s elections, instead they campaigned as three main blocs. That gave voters opposed to the PiS government a genuine choice, and likely played a big part in the record turnout that helped bring Tusk’s coalition to power. It is similarly possible now that a four-branched opposition, ranging from Morawiecki on the centre right, through PiS and Confederation, to Braun on the radical right, could together win a parliamentary majority. Polls currently show those four groups with combined support of around 50% (though polling regarding support for Morawiecki’s prospective party should for now be treated with caution). Jestem dumny z tego, co wspólnie zrobiliśmy dla Polski. I wiem jedno – nasza misja wciąż trwa💪🇵🇱#RozwojPlus pic.twitter.com/xOnxKDoroS — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 31, 2026 However, even if they do win a majority, it is far from certain what would happen then. In 2023, the three opposition blocs were, although standing separately, clearly aligned with one another and focused on removing PiS from power. When they together won a parliamentary majority, it was absolutely clear they would form a coalition government. By contrast, today’s opposition is deeply divided. Confederation and KKP regularly attack PiS. It is not at all clear that Confederation would be willing to form a coalition government with PiS, while Kaczyński has explicitly ruled out working with the pro-Russian, anti-American Braun. Meanwhile, Morawiecki’s split has followed months of bitter infighting within PiS, which has often been carried out in public. The manner in which he and his allies are now departing the party means that relations with PiS are likely to remain difficult. The national-conservative opposition PiS party's newly named candidate for prime minister has made overtures to the far-right Confederation. But he also ruled out Grzegorz Braun, an even more radical far-right figure, serving in a PiS-led government https://t.co/i3zOZJWdUN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 9, 2026 It would therefore be hard for the opposition to form a government, even if they do win a majority. In this situation, the role of President Karol Nawrocki may be vital. Though elected with the support of PiS last year, he was technically an independent and maintained good relations with Confederation and even, to some extent, Braun (who endorsed Nawrocki after being eliminated in the first round). When Morawiecki this week announced the “ten pillars” of Development Plus’s programme, he made clear his loyalty to Nawrocki: the second of those pillars is “respect for the president”. Nie ma silnej Polski bez wielkich ambicji. Nie ma wielkich ambicji bez ludzi, którzy je zdefiniują i będą gotowi wziąć odpowiedzialność za ich realizację. Bezpieczeństwo. Rozwój. Suwerenność. Ambicja. Tożsamość. Patriotyzm. To nie hasła wyborcze, ale fundamenty państwa, które… pic.twitter.com/G0YBbfhLye — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 28, 2026 Many on the right hope that Nawrocki can play a role next year in helping the opposition present a more united front during the election campaign. It is also the president who decides who gets the opportunity to try to form a government after the elections. That role would be of particular significance if, as is very possible, Tusk’s KO emerges as the biggest individual party but the opposition together may be able to form a parliamentary majority. Given that we are still over 14 months away from the elections, and Morawiecki has not even yet officially split from PiS, it is still far too early to make confident predictions. However, while Morawiecki’s likely departure is clearly a personal blow to Kaczyński – and a sign of the 77-year-old’s waning influence over not only the Polish right but even his own party – it may conversely provide a boost to the opposition as a whole. Poland has banned children from using smartphones and other electronic devices in primary schools and kindergartens in a bid to improve their wellbeing and safety. The new legislation, signed into law by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki on Thursday, will take effect at the start of the school year on 1 September, but schools will have until the end of 2026 to adjust. Prezydent podpisał nowelizację, która zakazuje korzystania z telefonów komórkowych w przedszkolach i szkołach. (PAP)#PAPInformacje pic.twitter.com/CK7YFU7sru — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) July 30, 2026 Under the new rules, pupils in primary schools and kindergartens will be prohibited from using smartphones and other electronic devices allowing communication or audio and video recording for the entire school day, including breaks and lessons held outside of school grounds. Schools will be allowed, but not required, to create designated places where pupils’ devices can be stored in a safe way and with respect for their privacy. The law, however, allows for some exceptions. When pupils need a device because of illness, disability or other special needs, school headteachers can permit their use. Phones could also be used in emergencies where there is a direct threat to life, health or property. Furthermore, pupils will be permitted to use mobile phones if a teacher deems them necessary for educational purposes and gives approval. The law also allows secondary schools to introduce bans on smartphone use if they choose, but does not make this compulsory, with such schools retaining autonomy to set their own rules through their statutes. The draft law banning phones from primary schools was first approved by the government in June. It then went to the Sejm, the lower and more powerful chamber of Poland’s parliament, which introduced amendments, including extending the measures to kindergartens. The Sejm then approved the bill in a rare near-unanimous vote, with only some MPs from the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) voting against it. Subsequently, the Senate passed the bill without amendments, sending it to Nawrocki, who could have signed it, vetoed it, or sent it to Poland’s constitutional court for review. Poland’s government has approved a ban on mobile phones in primary schools as well as tougher age-verification requirements for online pornography. Both measures still require parliamentary and presidential approval before becoming law https://t.co/y4Ycf46FQD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2026 The president ultimately decided to sign the law, with his office noting that the measures aim to “create safer learning conditions” and support the “healthy and responsible” use of digital technologies by pupils. Poland’s education minister Barbara Nowacka said last month that the law would “improve teachers’ power, autonomy and agency, as well as order and digital wellbeing in schools”. She added that, although many schools already have such bans in place, teachers had asked for legal backing to help enforce them. He is banned from re-entering Poland and the Schengen area for five years. The 34-year-old was charged with promoting Nazism, an offence carrying a maximum sentence of three years in prison, and desecration of a memorial site. “A place that symbolises one of the greatest tragedies in human history requires special respect, and insulting it does not go without consequences,” said the border guard. @PolskaPolicja zatrzymała ob. A police probe found that the man, who had been living and working in the Wielkopolska province, had “posed for a photo making the Nazi salute” at the museum while visiting it. Prosecutors were informed of the case, police said, adding that the man was subsequently charged with two crimes: public promotion of Nazism and the desecration of a memorial site. He admitted to the offences and voluntarily submitted to his punishment, which consisted of a 2,000 zloty (€464) fine along with a decision for his verdict to be made public, they added. He was then handed over to Poland’s border guard, which decided to deport him and ban him from entering Poland and other Schengen countries for five years. The border guard said that the decision was “immediately enforceable”, and was based on “considerations of security and public order as well as the interests of the Republic of Poland.” It also noted that a court decided to place the man in a facility for foreigners in the city of Przemyśl, where he will await deportation. Poland’s government has appointed a marketing and branding expert to develop a unified strategy for promoting the country abroad, saying the move will help boost tourism, support Polish products and attract foreign investment. Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, a professor at Wrocław University of Economics, noted that her appointment signals “a shift” from simple promotional activities to “managing the reputation of our great country”. The move comes as Poland seeks to capitalise on its economic success, including growth in tourism and continued investments. But the government says that current promotion efforts lack a single strategy and are fragmented. Czas na markę Polska! Witamy na pokładzie prof. Barbarę Mróz – Gorgoń 🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/PPX2eWTRSm — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 29, 2026 Last year, Poland’s sport and tourism ministry appointed Mróz-Gorgoń, who also advises companies and institutions on branding strategy and founded a think tank dedicated to promoting Poland, to an interministerial team tasked with developing a comprehensive new branding strategy for Poland. The government said, however, that efforts to promote Poland were so far fragmented and lacked a single strategy, which is why it created the post of commissioner for promotion of the Poland brand. As the first specialist to take the position, Mróz-Gorgoń will be tasked with preparing a strategy to build a national brand and help implement it, coordinate activities to help grow tourism, support investments, and improve Poland’s position on the world stage. “We will create one programme resulting in the joint promotion of our country’s brand,” said Tusk. According to the government, this will come at no further cost, but ensure that existing funds will be spent in a more “coherent and effective way”. Mróz-Gorgoń, meanwhile, noted that “the Poland brand is not the property of the government. It is created by entrepreneurs, artists, athletes, local governments and millions of Poles at home and abroad”. Developing this brand “means more investment, recognition of our brands and products abroad, and it also provides greater strength in international relations,” she continued. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 Poland has been one of the world’s fastest-growing economies in recent decades. Last year, the sport and tourism ministry announced that it wants tourism to contribute 9% of GDP annually within a decade, from about 5% now, and for Poland to become a leader in the sector in central and eastern Europe. Foreign direct investment in Poland grew from just under 15.5 billion zloty in 2003, a year before the country joined the European Union, to around 61.3 billion zloty last year, according to figures from the National Bank of Poland (NBP). Various state and private companies – such as delivery giant InPost, insurer PZU, and train manufacturer Pesa – are establishing themselves abroad by buying some of their rivals. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday that Polish airspace had been violated during a massive missile attack by Russia on western Ukraine overnight, adding that there were no casualties or immediate threat to civilians. A suspected Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashed in eastern Poland, around 100 km from the Ukrainian border, prompting the deployment of police counter-terrorism officers and other security services to the site. The fall of the object, which is reported to have caused a powerful explosion, left a crater about 10 metres wide and scattered fragments in a field between Tarnawa-Kolonia and Tokary in Lublin province, about 2 km from the nearest buildings, according to local police. World.title: Record number of Poles opposed to Ukraine’s EU membership
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Support for Ukraine joining the European Union has fallen sharply in Poland, with opposition reaching a record high of 40%, a survey carried out by the Polish state research agency CBOS shows. The figures show that 50% of Poles still support Ukraine’s EU membership, but that is a significant decline from 74% in October 2023, when the question was last asked, and from a record 90% in March 2022, shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The shift comes as public sentiment towards Ukrainians in general in Poland has deteriorated in recent years. The latest CBOS poll shows that, among those who support Ukraine’s EU accession, most favour a gradual process, with 41% of all respondents saying Ukraine should join the EU but “without undue haste”. “Only 9% of respondents currently support Ukraine’s earliest possible EU membership, which is the lowest figure in the history of these surveys,” CBOS reported. Meanwhile, opposition to Ukraine’s EU membership has increased by 23 percentage points since October 2023, reaching its highest level in the history of CBOS surveys. People with right-wing political beliefs are most likely to be opposed to Ukraine’s accession (53%), while the age group with the highest percentage of people opposed is those aged 18-24 (58%). The survey also found that a majority of Poles expect the war in Ukraine to end with territorial concessions from Kyiv – 55% of respondents said they believed Ukraine would lose some territory, a view that has remained dominant since December 2024. Compared with the previous survey, however, pessimism has eased. The proportion of respondents who expect Ukraine to lose part of its territory fell by 8 percentage points, while the number expecting Russia to take control of the entire country declined from 8% to 6%. On Western support for Ukraine, 39% of respondents said the military, financial and humanitarian assistance provided by countries in the West was sufficient. Meanwhile, 27% said aid was excessive, while 22% said it was insufficient. Russia has published purported archival documents relating to massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. Kyiv had warned that Russia was planning to release the files in order to stir tensions, while Polish media note that the material contains nothing new https://t.co/CI0cfAlDle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 6, 2026 Ukrainians are Poland’s largest foreign national group, with almost 1.6 million living in the country, but recent polls have shown growing hostility towards them, fuelled in part by anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from far-right parties and a tougher stance towards Kyiv from some opposition politicians. In its annual survey of attitudes towards national and ethnic groups, CBOS found earlier this year that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians increased by five percentage points this year, the largest rise recorded among all groups surveyed, reaching 43%. Tensions between the two countries have also been heightened by disputes over historical issues and a series of recent incidents targeting Ukrainians in Poland. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians rose by 30% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to newly reported police data. Last weekend, three men were filmed violently attacking a Ukrainian woman and her partner outside a shop in Wrocław, apparently because of her accent. Two of the assailants have since been detained by police, while their victims required treatment in hospital. In response, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for Poles to “wage war on violence”, saying that the perpetrators of such acts “have become emboldened precisely because they now have political role models, political patrons, and political support”. World.title: Spaniard Santi Denia Named Coach of the Czech Republic National Team
World.content:
Spanish coach Santi Denia took over the Czech Republic national team on Friday to become the first foreigner in the post.

The Czech soccer association said the 52-year-old signed a two-year contract with an option to be extended by another two years.

Czech football association head David Trunda introduced Denia at a news conference in Prague.

“We greatly appreciate that an expert with such a credit and immense experience at the international level is joining the Czech national team,” Trunda said.



“I’m happy to be here and I’m extremely motivated, because I consider it a great opportunity to lead the Czech national team,” Denia said. “Czech football has a magnificent history and I honestly regard it as a great honor to be here.”

Denia replaced Miroslav Koubek who resigned after the team’s early exit from the World Cup.

Denia was a center-back in Atletico Madrid (1994-2005) and has two games on the national team to his credit.

As coach, he led Spain to gold at the 2024 Paris Olympics. He also claimed the European titles with Spain´s under-17 (2017) and under-19 teams (2019).

He was most recently in charge of Al-Shahania, a club in Qatar.

His first major task in the post will be to face tough opponents in League A of the Nations League. The Czechs open the competition by hosting Croatia on Sept. 26 in a group which also includes England and World Cup champions Spain.

World.title: Czech PM Calls for Closing Schengen to Spain due to Migration Crisis in Ceuta
World.content:
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš called for temporarily excluding Spain from Schengen due to the migration crisis in Ceuta, where about 49,000 migrants entered uncontrollably from Morocco.

Italy has already suspended Schengen rules in connection with Spain.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš called for closing the Schengen zone to Spain after a sharp escalation of the migration crisis in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta.

According to Babiš, the situation in Ceuta is “absolutely scandalous,” and the cause of the crisis was the overly lenient migration policy of the Spanish authorities.



According to the publication, since Thursday, about 49,000 migrants have entered Ceuta uncontrollably from the territory of Morocco. At least 19 people have died trying to cross the maritime border.

Foreign Minister Petr Macinka (Motorists) described the situation as a serious challenge for the entire Schengen Area but stopped short of calling for Spain’s exclusion, saying he wanted to hear Madrid’s position before drawing conclusions.

What is the Schengen Agreement?

The Schengen Area allows people to travel between 29 European countries without routine passport checks at internal borders.

While border controls are normally abolished, member states can temporarily reinstate them if they believe there is a serious threat to public order or internal security.

Italy does not share a land border with Spain, so the decision to reintroduce border controls for a month will impact people travelling by plane or boat between the two countries.

Where is Ceuta?

Ceuta is an autonomous Spanish city on the northern coast of Africa that borders Morocco.

Spain also controls the nearby city of Melilla. Together, the two enclaves form the European Union’s only land borders with Africa.

Roughly the size of inner Sydney, Ceuta has a population of just over 83,000, according to Spain’s Instituto Nacional de Estadistica. It is home to Christian and Muslim communities, including Spanish and Moroccan residents and cross-border workers.

World.title: Prague’s Online Heat Map Shows Where to Find Water and Shade
World.content:
As another spell of extreme summer heat approaches the Czech Republic, Prague has published an online map showing where residents can cool down, find drinking water or spend time near water.

Temperatures in the capital could reach 38°C, with the hottest conditions expected toward the end of the week.

This map is designed to help people find relief across the city and includes public drinking fountains, misting systems, fountains, wells and locations suitable for swimming or relaxing beside the water.

The project was prepared by the City of Prague in cooperation with the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR Prague) and the municipal technology company Operátor ICT.



The initiative is part of the city’s broader efforts to prepare for more frequent periods of extreme heat. Prague says it is increasingly focusing on measures that can reduce the effects of rising temperatures over the longer term, rather than relying only on temporary interventions.

More trees, water and shade planned

Prague is also looking to incorporate more greenery and water into public spaces as part of new development projects.

The city is supporting measures including new fountains and other water features, green roofs, rainwater collection tanks, climbing plants, permeable surfaces and additional tree planting. The expansion of parks is also among the measures being considered.

Temperatures could approach 40°C

The current heatwave is expected to reach its peak on Friday, when temperatures could climb as high as 39°C in parts of the Czech Republic.

Friday night could also remain exceptionally warm, with overnight temperatures staying above 20°C in some areas.

A temporary change is expected on Saturday, particularly in parts of the country where showers and thunderstorms could bring some relief. The cooler conditions, however, are not expected to last.

At the beginning of next week, temperatures are forecast to rise again, with daytime highs between 32°C and 37°C.

World.title: Canadian International High School in Prague: Your Pathway to Top Universities Worldwide
World.content:
Earning an internationally recognized high school diploma and preparing for admission to top universities no longer requires moving abroad.

Canadian International High School in Prague (CIHS) offers students in Grades 10-12 a fully English-language education based on the Canadian curriculum.

Located in the heart of Prague, CIHS combines the strengths of Canada’s education system with the quality of life and accessibility of the Czech Republic. Students receive a globally recognized diploma while studying in a familiar European environment, avoiding the higher costs and challenges of relocating overseas.

An International Diploma Recognized Worldwide

Graduates earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma (OSSD), Canada’s official high school credential, recognized in more than 20 countries. The diploma provides access to over 30,000 universities and colleges worldwide, including leading institutions across Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Europe.

Unlike the Czech education system, which typically spans 13 years, the Canadian program is completed in 12. As a result, students graduate a year earlier, begin university sooner, and gain an additional advantage as they build their academic and professional future.

Learning the Canadian Way

CIHS delivers its academic program in partnership with Toronto Imperial School, ensuring that students follow authentic Canadian educational standards. Courses are taught using modern curricula, teaching methods, and learning resources aligned with those used in Ontario schools.

English is the language of instruction across all subjects. An international faculty, including teachers from Canada, creates an immersive English-speaking environment that helps students strengthen their academic language skills and confidently transition into universities abroad.

To maintain high academic standards, all teachers undergo a rigorous selection process followed by professional training led by Canadian educators and the school’s academic partners.

Outstanding Value

Tuition is, on average, two to three times lower than at many international schools in Prague while offering an extensive range of included benefits.

Tuition covers:

the Ontario Secondary School Diploma (OSSD)

an iPad for both academic and personal use

for both academic and personal use a complete school uniform

an annual gym membership

continuous academic guidance and support

and support educational trips to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and Germany

to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and Germany participation in the Exchange program in the United States.

International Experience Beyond the Classroom

Education at CIHS extends well beyond the classroom. Each semester, students have the opportunity to join educational trips to Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Switzerland, and other destinations. These experiences include university campus visits, meetings with admissions representatives, and valuable insight into international higher education systems.

Students may also participate in the Exchange USA program, spending one or two semesters at one of 40 partner high schools across the United States. The program offers full immersion in American school life while strengthening English proficiency and developing valuable intercultural experience.

For students planning to continue their education in the U.S., CIHS also offers the opportunity to transfer to an American high school during Grade 12 on an F-1 student visa, complete their final year there, and graduate with a U.S. high school diploma.

A Modern Campus in Central Prague

The school is located in Holešovice, one of Prague’s fastest-growing and most vibrant districts. Its central location makes the campus easily accessible from virtually any part of the city by public transportation, while convenient parking is available for families.

The campus occupies a modern business complex close to parks and the Vltava riverfront, providing an ideal balance between study and recreation. Students also benefit from an on-site cafeteria and access to medical professionals, including general practitioners, dermatologists, immunologists, and allergists. Sports facilities, swimming pools, cafés, and shops are all within walking distance.

Personalized University Preparation

Beginning after Grade 10, students choose one of two academic pathways: Business & Social Science or Engineering, allowing them to focus on subjects aligned with their future university studies.

Throughout the program, experienced teachers and academic advisors provide personalized guidance, helping students develop essential academic skills, explore career options, and build competitive university applications.

Graduate Outcomes

By the time they graduate, CIHS students have gained far more than a high school diploma. They leave with:

the internationally recognized Ontario Secondary School Diploma

strong academic English proficiency

experience studying in an international environment

university admissions guidance

a global network of peers

participation in international educational programs

access to leading universities across Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe, and beyond.

Canadian International High School in Prague welcomes prospective students and their families to visit the campus, meet the faculty, and learn more about its Canadian curriculum.

It’s an opportunity to experience a truly international education and earn a globally recognized diploma – while staying in the heart of Europe.

World.title: Prague Pride Strengthens Security Measures Following Berlin Attack
World.content:
Security will be tightened at this year’s Prague Pride festival following a deadly attack at a similar event in Berlin.

Czech police are preparing additional measures to protect participants in the week-long festival, which begins Monday.

The measures will also reflect changes to this year’s festival route and venue.

Prague Pride is moving its main festival area from Letná Plain to Štvanice Island. The traditional Saturday parade will also follow a new route, starting in the lower section of Wenceslas Square, continuing through the historic center and ending at Štvanice.



Organizers will begin the parade with a minute of silence on Wenceslas Square to remember the person killed in the Berlin attack.

“Thousands of people standing in silence will be a reminder that we will definitely not remain silent about violence motivated by prejudice,” Prague Pride director Kamila Fröhlichová said.

This year’s Prague Pride will feature more than 100 cultural, educational and social events. Dozens of associations, institutions, companies and individuals will organize programs at venues across the capital.

While many events will focus on the lives and experiences of LGBTQ+ people, the festival will also address wider questions surrounding human rights and civil society. A full program is available on the Prague Pride website.

Prague Pride was first held in August 2011. Its inaugural edition was met with strong opposition from conservative groups and politicians, who described the parade as obscene and accused its organizers of promoting what they called an “ideology of homosexuality.”

Then-President Václav Klaus was among the most prominent critics, arguing that society needed to oppose what he described as the spread of homosexuality.

Protests continued in subsequent years but gradually declined in size and intensity.

World.title: Prague Opens Air-Conditioned Space in City Centre to Help Beat Heat Wave
World.content:
People looking for relief from the heat in central Prague can use the air-conditioned ground floor of the Škoda Palace in Jungmannova Street on Thursday and Friday.

The city has opened the space to the public as temperatures across the Czech Republic are expected to rise well above 30°C. The building will be accessible from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. on both days.

Visitors can sit on benches and chairs, refill their water bottles at drinking fountains and use the toilets. Drinks and snacks are also available for purchase.



The measure comes as the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute has warned of very high temperatures in parts of the country. Forecasters are advising people to drink regularly, stay out of direct sunlight where possible and avoid strenuous physical activity, particularly during the afternoon.

The Czech Republic is facing several days of intense heat, with Friday expected to be among the hottest day of the current spell. Temperatures above 35°C are possible in some areas.

Individual Prague districts are taking similar steps. Prague 3, for example, plans to make air-conditioned areas in its town hall, information centre and Žižkostel available to the public when temperatures are forecast to exceed 35°C. Visitors will be able to sit down, drink water and take a break from the heat.

The city says the cooling spaces are intended to provide temporary relief during the hottest periods, particularly for people who may struggle to cope with high temperatures.

World.title: Revolut Opens Private Market Funds to Czech Investors
World.content:
Revolut is expanding its investment services in the Czech Republic, giving retail customers access to funds focused on private equity, private credit and infrastructure.

The new products will become available in the Revolut app from July 31. The fintech has signed distribution agreements with four major asset managers — Apollo, Ares, Hamilton Lane and Partners Group — which collectively manage more than $2.8 trillion in assets.

The move gives Czech retail investors access to parts of the private markets that have traditionally been aimed largely at institutional investors.



Private market investments have often required substantial minimum commitments, frequently above €100,000, or around CZK 2.5 million. Revolut’s new offering is designed to lower that barrier and allow customers to add private assets to portfolios that may already include stocks, bonds and exchange-traded funds.

Investments will be available directly through the Revolut app.

The funds will be offered through the European Long-Term Investment Fund framework, known as ELTIF 2.0.

How ELTIF 2.0 works

The structure is intended to provide investors with greater flexibility than traditional private equity funds, where capital can remain committed for several years and withdrawals may not be possible during that period.

The products offered through Revolut use an “evergreen” structure. This allows investors to put money into funds with existing portfolios rather than waiting for a traditional investment cycle to begin.

ELTIF 2.0 also provides scheduled liquidity windows during which investors can request the redemption of their holdings, subject to the conditions of the individual fund.

That does not mean the investments are as liquid as publicly traded shares. Private market assets remain difficult to sell quickly, and investors should expect to hold their money for the long term.

Revolut already offers Czech customers access to a range of traditional investments, including US and European stocks, ETFs, bonds and commodities. The addition of private market funds expands the investment options available through the same app.

World.title: From Old Town to Main Station: Tourist Charged €150 for Short Taxi Ride
World.content:
A tourist has reported an alleged taxi scam in Prague, claiming that a journey from Old Town Square to Prague Main Railway Station ended with an unexpectedly high fare and a disputed payment.

The incident reportedly took place on July 25 at around 16:15. According to the complaint, the driver charged CZK 980 for the ride, an amount the passenger said was far higher than the expected price for such a short distance.

The tourist claims that the driver refused to accept payment by card and requested cash instead.



“I paid him 100 Euros for the fare. He just took the note, swapped it and lied to me saying what I gave was 100 in Czech currency, and demanded me to pay the remaining 50 euro taxi fare,” the tourist said in his complaint.

“So I paid the initial 100 euro that was swapped, plus the 50 euro taxi fare.”

According to the passenger, the total amount paid for the ride was therefore €150 (over 3,600 CZK). He said he was rushing to catch a train to Bratislava and was unable to resolve the dispute at the scene.

The tourist also claimed that no receipt was provided after the payment. According to his account, the driver said an invoice would be sent by email, but it was never received.

The case has been reported to the relevant authorities, while details of the incident have also been shared online to raise awareness among other visitors.

Travellers are also encouraged to use established taxi applications or services recommended by hotels, restaurants, and official tourist information centres. Paying by card and confirming the expected price in advance can help avoid disputes.

World.title: Hungary joins 21 EU leaders in criticism of Spain’s migration response after mass arrivals
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has joined 21 other European leaders in signing a joint letter criticising Spain’s handling of a recent migration surge, warning that recent developments could undermine the protection of the European Union’s external borders.

The initiative follows reports that nearly 50,000 irregular migrants crossed into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco over recent days, prompting calls for a coordinated European response.

Joint letter urges stronger EU border protection

According to Foreign Minister Anita Orbán, the 22 heads of state and government argue that the Spanish government’s response risks weakening the EU’s external border controls.

The letter reportedly calls for coordinated action at EU level to strengthen border protection and warns against creating the impression that entering the bloc illegally could eventually lead to legal residency.

The signatories also said they are prepared to consider temporarily reintroducing internal border controls within the Schengen Area if necessary.

Hungarian government links surge to Spanish court ruling

In a Facebook post, Orbán said the recent events recalled the 2015 migration crisis, when Europe experienced large-scale irregular border crossings.

She also suggested that a ruling issued earlier this month by Spain’s Supreme Court may have contributed to the recent surge. According to the Hungarian government’s account, the court ruled that people arriving by sea could not be immediately returned, a decision the signatories believe may have encouraged further crossings.

Spain says most arrivals have already returned

Orbán said she had been in continuous contact with her European counterparts and that Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares confirmed that around 49,000 people had already returned to Morocco. Nevertheless, she argued that the scale of the incident justified the joint appeal by the 22 European leaders.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

Calls for emergency EU coordination

The signatories are urging the Irish Presidency of the Council of the European Union to convene an emergency video conference of EU interior ministers to coordinate the bloc’s response. They are also calling for stronger support from Frontex, the EU’s border and coast guard agency, and a review of cooperation with Morocco on migration management.

Hungary reiterates opposition to illegal migration

Orbán said every EU member state, including Spain, shares responsibility for protecting the Union’s external borders. “The Hungarian government will continue to stand firmly against illegal migration and defend Hungary’s borders under all circumstances,” she wrote.

World.title: Budapest taxi fares rise from today – airport pickups also become more expensive
World.content:
Travelling by taxi in Budapest now costs more after new official fares came into force. The changes include higher base and distance charges, while passengers travelling to or from Budapest Airport will also have to pay a new airport surcharge. At the same time, another change affecting airport taxi operations is set to take effect within days.

Higher official taxi fares now in effect

Budapest’s revised taxi tariff officially entered into force today following an amendment to the city’s taxi regulations. (1 EUR = 365 HUF) The new official fares are:

Base fare: increased from HUF 1,100 to HUF 1,300

increased from Per-kilometre fare: increased from HUF 440 to HUF 521

increased from Per-minute fare: increased from HUF 110 to HUF 130

The fare increase was approved by the Budapest General Assembly at its 26 June meeting.

New airport surcharge introduced

Passengers travelling to or from Budapest Ferenc Liszt International Airport will also notice a new fixed airport charge. A new HUF 800 airport fee has been introduced, bringing the starting fare for airport journeys to HUF 2,100. The surcharge applies to trips beginning or ending at the airport.

Photo: Budapest Airport

Airport access changes could affect some taxi passengers

A separate issue could soon affect how passengers are picked up and dropped off at the airport. According to the Budapest Taxi Association, from 3 August Budapest Airport will end the current five-minute free transit period through its airport car parks for most taxi operators. The association says that, without free access, many taxis would have to pay parking fees every time they enter the terminal area.

As a result, many independent taxi operators may have to use a designated taxi parking area located around 1.1 kilometres from Terminal 2, meaning some passengers could face a considerably longer walk with their luggage.

Főtaxi services remain unchanged

According to VG.hu, the reported changes do not affect Főtaxi, which continues to hold the concession to provide official taxi services from Budapest Airport until 2030. Its vehicles will continue to pick up arriving passengers directly outside the terminals.

The Budapest Taxi Association has urged the airport operator to suspend the new access rules until an agreement can be reached, arguing that the immediate introduction could reduce service quality and inconvenience travellers. According to the association, Budapest Airport has declined to postpone the measure.

What travellers should know

Visitors arriving in Budapest should be aware of two separate changes:

Taxi journeys across Budapest now cost more under the revised official tariff.

From 3 August, passengers using non-contracted taxi companies at the airport could encounter different pickup arrangements if the new access rules take effect as planned.

World.title: Hungary launches investigation into relocation of Slovak Roma families
World.content:
Hungary’s Interior Ministry has announced an official investigation into the controversial relocation of Slovak Roma families to the village of Szalonna and nearby settlements in north-eastern Hungary, saying it will examine who organised and financed the moves and whether any legal violations occurred.

The announcement follows reports of families relocating from the Lubina settlement in Košice, Slovakia, after authorities began clearing the informal housing area.

Government to scrutinise property purchases and loans

In a statement to Hungarian news outlet Telex, the Interior Ministry said it was taking both the concerns of local residents and the safety and human dignity of the relocated families seriously. The investigation will seek to establish:

who organised and financed the relocations;

how the property purchases were arranged;

what loan agreements were signed;

whether any coercion, deception, abuse of vulnerable persons, financial misconduct or other legal violations occurred.

The ministry stressed that, in its view, the issue is not an ethnic or nationality matter, but rather one of legality and transparency. Authorities will examine whether the relocations and property transactions were carried out lawfully, transparently and with the families’ free consent.

Hungary calls for joint action with Slovakia

The Interior Ministry said the situation cannot be resolved through isolated local measures alone and instead requires close cooperation between the Hungarian and Slovak governments and their respective authorities.

However, the ministry did not confirm whether it has already contacted the municipality of Košice or Slovak government officials, nor whether any bilateral discussions have begun. It also said it would refrain from treating unverified figures, political accusations or speculation as fact until the investigation is completed.

The controversy over families relocating from Košice

The issue gained national attention after reports emerged that several Slovak-speaking Roma families living in deep poverty had purchased homes in Szalonna after leaving the Lubina settlement near Košice, which is being demolished.

According to Slovak municipal officials, residents of the settlement were offered alternative housing options, although the authorities have not disclosed where those alternatives are located.

The relocation has triggered concern among local leaders in north-eastern Hungary, some of whom fear that larger numbers of families could arrive in the coming months. Slovak officials, meanwhile, have denied that any government-organised or municipally funded mass relocation programme exists, insisting that the moves are voluntary and privately arranged.

The mayor of Košice’s Terasa district has previously stated that the homes were purchased by the families themselves, in some cases with loans provided through a civic association established to support disadvantaged households seeking a fresh start.

World.title: Hungary prepares emergency power restrictions, Paks nuclear plant could shut down this weekend
World.content:
Hungary has announced further emergency energy-saving measures after Prime Minister Péter Magyar warned that the Paks Nuclear Power Plant may have to shut down completely as early as this weekend due to the exceptionally low level of the River Danube.

In a video statement released on Saturday morning following an overnight meeting of the government’s emergency task force, Magyar said the country was facing an extraordinary situation requiring immediate action.

Paks output falls to just 480 MW

According to the prime minister, Paks’ output has already been reduced dramatically. “During the night and early morning we had to reduce the plant’s capacity once again. It is currently producing only 480 megawatts, compared with its normal 2,000 megawatts,” Magyar said.

He added that the national electricity transmission system operator MAVIR has activated its emergency protocol for major disturbances to the electricity grid.

The government now expects the plant could be shut down completely earlier than previously forecast, possibly during the weekend rather than early next week. Meanwhile, auxiliary power stations remain on standby, and the repaired unit at the Dunamenti Power Plant is expected to return to service on Sunday, helping offset part of the lost generation capacity.

Large industrial consumers face mandatory power cuts

The government has also adopted a new emergency decree changing how electricity restrictions would be implemented if supply shortages worsen.

Until now, large industrial users have voluntarily reduced consumption, collectively cutting demand by around 240 MW. However, the government believes that will no longer be sufficient if Paks loses additional generating capacity. Under the new rules:

major electricity users will first be asked to reduce consumption voluntarily;

companies failing to meet their commitments may face sanctions;

after prior warning, MAVIR will be able to order mandatory consumption reductions;

certain large consumers may be temporarily disconnected from the grid if necessary.

Magyar stressed that households would remain the last group to face any potential electricity restrictions. He also announced a temporary expansion of grid access for household solar panel systems, allowing more residential producers to feed electricity back into the national grid to reduce reliance on expensive imports.

Rail freight halted during evening peak

The government also approved several additional emergency measures. From Monday, rail freight services will be suspended between 5:00 PM and 10:00 PM, when electricity demand is highest.

Home working will be introduced across the public administration during the first three days of next week wherever operationally possible, while private employers are being encouraged to adopt similar arrangements to reduce office energy consumption.

The decorative lighting of all state-owned buildings will also be switched off.

Water restrictions tightened

The government has also ordered stricter water-saving measures as the drought continues. Water authorities have been instructed to introduce the highest level of water restrictions wherever necessary. The measures include a ban on watering sports grounds and filling swimming pools, while residents are also being urged to avoid unnecessary water use.

Government blames previous administration

Magyar again criticised the previous government, arguing that the risks posed by extremely low Danube water levels had been known since the record drought of 2018. He said critical upgrades to Paks’ pumping systems had been delayed for years, while water infrastructure had also been neglected, leaving the country more vulnerable to the current crisis.

World.title: Budapest slows trams and metro trains to cut electricity use during energy crisis
World.content:
Budapest will introduce slower metro and tram services in the coming days as part of emergency measures to reduce electricity consumption during Hungary’s deepening energy crisis.

Mayor Gergely Karácsony announced on Facebook that the capital’s public transport companies had reviewed how they could contribute to energy savings while minimising disruption for passengers. Under the new timetable, metro trains and trams will accelerate more gradually, slightly increasing journey times but reducing electricity consumption by around 15 megawatt-hours per day.

Some trolleybuses replaced with diesel buses

The city will also temporarily replace electric trolleybuses on certain weekday routes with modern diesel buses equipped with efficient air conditioning. According to the mayor, the measures are designed to support the stability of Budapest’s electricity supply during what the government has described as one of Hungary’s most challenging energy situations in decades.

“Let’s take care of one another,” Karácsony wrote in his message.

BKK announces additional measures

The Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) said it would also adjust the charging schedule of the capital’s electric buses in cooperation with ArrivaBus, ensuring they are not charged during the critical evening peak between 5:00 PM and 10:00 PM.

In addition, the electric bicycles of the MOL Bubi bike-sharing system will be charged outside the evening peak period after service hours.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

Part of nationwide energy-saving campaign

The capital’s announcement comes as Prime Minister Péter Magyar has repeatedly urged households, businesses and public institutions to reduce electricity consumption, particularly during the evening peak demand period.

The government recently established a national energy operations unit to prepare for various emergency scenarios as concerns grow over the impact of the exceptionally low water level of the River Danube on the operation of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.

Authorities have stressed that any emergency restrictions, if necessary, would primarily target large industrial consumers rather than essential public services such as hospitals or social care institutions.

World.title: Serbia’s president to discuss major MOL oil deal with Péter Magyar and Vladimir Putin
World.content:
Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić has announced that he expects to hold talks with both Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Russian President Vladimir Putin in the coming days as negotiations over the future ownership of Serbia’s oil company enter a decisive stage.

Vučić said he expects an agreement on the sale of the Russian stake in Serbia’s oil company, NIS, to be finalised soon, with Hungary’s MOL Group seeking to acquire a majority interest currently held by Russian energy giant Gazprom Neft.

MOL receives fresh US approval to continue negotiations

In a separate announcement on Friday evening, MOL said it had received a new authorisation from the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), allowing it to continue negotiations over the acquisition until 28 August 2026.

The previous licence, granted in early July, had been due to expire on 31 July 2026.

The approval enables MOL to continue talks despite US sanctions imposed on NIS in October 2025, which targeted the Serbian company because of its Russian majority ownership.

Major ownership change under discussion

MOL signed a binding framework agreement with Gazprom Neft in January 2026 outlining the key terms for purchasing a 56.15% stake in NIS.

Negotiations between the two companies are continuing, while MOL is also in discussions with Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), the United Arab Emirates’ national oil company, over a possible minority investment in NIS.

According to the current ownership structure:

Gazprom Neft holds 44.9% of NIS.

Gazprom owns a further 11.3%.

The Serbian government controls 29.87%.

The remaining shares are held by minority shareholders.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

Strategic importance for the region

The outcome of the negotiations is being closely watched across Central and Southeast Europe, as NIS plays a significant role in the regional fuel market.

If completed, the transaction would substantially expand MOL’s presence in the Western Balkans while reducing Russian ownership of one of Serbia’s most strategically important energy companies. The deal remains subject to ongoing negotiations, regulatory approvals and the relevant international sanctions framework.

World.title: Ghost bridge emerges from the Danube: Extreme drought reveals long-lost WWII relic in Budapest
World.content:
The Danube’s exceptionally low water level has revealed the remains of Budapest’s original Franz Joseph Bridge, offering a rare and striking glimpse into the city’s wartime past.

According to Falanszter, at the Liberty Bridge, visitors looking down into the river can once again spot structural elements of the bridge that collapsed into the Danube during the Second World War. The same remains last became visible during the record-low water levels of 2018.

A bridge with imperial origins and a wartime fate

The original bridge, officially named the Franz Joseph Bridge, was inaugurated on 4 October 1896 in the presence of Emperor Franz Joseph I, who famously drove the final ceremonial rivet into the structure himself, HVG writes. Tram services began crossing the bridge two years later.

During the Siege of Budapest in January 1945, retreating German forces destroyed the bridge to slow the advancing Soviet army. The central span collapsed into the Danube, where parts of the structure have remained ever since.

Following the war, the crossing became the first of Budapest’s destroyed Danube bridges to be rebuilt. It reopened on 20 August 1946 under its current name, the Liberty Bridge.

Low water levels continue to expose hidden history

The emergence of the bridge remains is the latest consequence of the Danube’s historically low water level, driven by prolonged drought and extreme heat.

Just last week, the low river level also exposed a Second World War explosive device near the central pier of Margaret Bridge. It was safely removed by Hungarian military bomb disposal experts.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

Experts have also warned that the falling river is creating heritage protection risks. As archaeological and historical objects become exposed, authorities are urging people not to move, collect or remove any artefacts they may discover along the riverbed.

In addition to their historical significance, some newly exposed sections of the riverbed are part of Budapest’s protected drinking water base, prompting officials to advise visitors to remain cautious when exploring the shoreline.

World.title: Here’s how much time Hungary’s Paks nuclear power plant may take to restart after unprecedented shutdown
World.content:
Restarting Hungary’s Paks Nuclear Power Plant could take up to a week if all four reactor units are shut down simultaneously, according to the plant’s Deputy CEO for Technical Affairs. The unprecedented situation is expected due to the record-low water level of the Danube, which has reduced the availability of cooling water.

Speaking to the Hungarian News Agency (MTI), László Nagy said that while shutting down an individual reactor is a relatively straightforward procedure, restarting the plant becomes significantly more complex if all four units have been out of operation for weeks.

A situation never seen before at Paks

Nagy explained that reactor shutdowns and restarts are routine at Paks, as each of the plant’s four units is taken offline roughly once a year for scheduled maintenance and refuelling.

However, this has never happened to all four reactors at the same time.

Under normal circumstances, the remaining operating reactors provide the steam needed to reheat equipment in the reactor being restarted. This process usually takes one to two days before the reactor can begin its physical start-up, followed by another one to two days before the unit reaches full generating capacity.

If every reactor has cooled down, however, there is no neighbouring unit available to provide auxiliary steam, making the restart of the first reactor much more complicated and considerably slower.

External electricity needed to heat the first reactor

Nagy recalled that when the plant first entered service, dedicated boilers were used to start the initial reactor. This time, following the anticipated shutdown, the plant will instead use its own existing equipment together with externally supplied electricity to heat the first reactor to the required operating temperature.

Once the reactor reaches the necessary temperature, the standard start-up procedure can begin. According to Nagy, the entire process of bringing the first unit back online and restoring operations could take up to one week.

Restart depends on Danube water levels

Even if heavy rainfall occurs across the Danube catchment area, the restart process cannot begin immediately. Nagy stressed that the plant can only begin reheating equipment once there is sufficient cooling water available at the Paks site itself. Until the Danube reaches an adequate water level, the restart procedure cannot even start.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

Gradual shutdown expected next week

Based on current water level forecasts, one of the two reactors still operating is expected to begin a gradual shutdown on Sunday evening. From Monday, only one reactor is expected to remain in operation, and even that unit will likely run below its nominal capacity, as only one of the eight pumps supplying cooling water from the Danube will remain operational.

According to the current forecast, the output of the final operating reactor will then be progressively reduced before it is shut down entirely around the middle of next week.

World.title: Nscale to acquire Romanian co-founded AI startup Anyscale in reportedly USD 1.65 billion deal
World.content:
Cloud infrastructure provider Nscale will acquire AI software startup Anyscale, which has Romanian-born university professor Ion Stoica among its co-founders, in a transaction worth roughly USD 1.65 billion, according to a Bloomberg News source.

Ion Stoica is a co-founder of Anyscale, together with Robert Nishihara (chief executive officer) and Philipp Moritz (chief technology officer), who were his PhD students at RISELab within the University of California, Berkeley.

San Francisco-based Anyscale provides software for organizing and managing complex AI workloads so that they can run smoothly across multiple computers simultaneously. Nscale said it expects to attract more customers by offering Anyscale’s software.

Anyscale will continue to operate under its own brand and serve its existing customers, the companies said. Anyscale’s entire team of approximately 200 people across the United States, Europe and India will join Nscale as part of the acquisition.

The transaction is expected to be completed in the second half of this year, the companies said.

Anyscale recorded revenue growth of 70% compared with the previous quarter in the company’s most recent quarter, according to a blog post by its co-founders.

Originally from Romania, Stoica left for the United States in the late 1990s to pursue his PhD at Carnegie Mellon University. Since 2000, he has been teaching at UC Berkeley, where he leads a laboratory funded largely by technology companies such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Google, and IBM, with an annual budget of more than USD 6 million.

Stoica became a billionaire by launching four startups that originated from his research laboratory at the University of California, Berkeley. The most valuable of them, Databricks and Anyscale, started as open-source projects within the university. The first was valued at USD 134 billion earlier this year.

Before Databricks, Stoica also co-founded video streaming startup Conviva.

World.title: UNICEF, Romanian Labor Ministry launch e-Learning HUB for professionals in social assistance
World.content:
Romania’s Labor Ministry and UNICEF announced the launch of e-Learning HUB, a national platform dedicated to the continuous professional training of personnel in the field of social services and sectors that contribute to social inclusion.

The HUB provides coordinated access to training opportunities, educational resources and professional development programs. The platform brings together continuous professional training opportunities for specialists in the social field, covering essential topics such as the protection of vulnerable persons, human rights, digital skills and quality standards in social services.

The HUB is designed to become the digital foundation of the future National Center for Continuous Training in Social Assistance, which is scheduled to become operational in 2028. The platform will contribute to increasing the skills of professionals in social assistance and related fields, personnel of central and local public authorities with responsibilities in the social field, decision-makers, accredited professional training providers, professional organizations, and non-governmental organizations active in the field of social assistance and the protection of human rights.

“Through e-Learning HUB, specialists across the country will be able to identify relevant courses more easily, develop their skills and have access to modern resources adapted to the real needs of the system,” said Silvia Dinică, State Secretary within the Labor Ministry.

“Professionals in social services are facing increasingly complex challenges, from poverty and social exclusion to the effects of recent crises on children and families. The e-Learning HUB platform offers a single access point to quality learning opportunities and represents an important step toward strengthening the workforce in the social field,” said Anna Riatti, UNICEF Representative in Romania.

The e-Learning HUB will facilitate access to accredited training programs, promote collaboration between institutions and training providers, and support the development of the skills needed to provide integrated and quality services.

World.title: North Bucharest Investments ANALYSIS | ANCPI Disruptions Slow the Market, but Housing Demand Remains Strong
World.content:
News from Companies

Against the backdrop of the ongoing operational disruption affecting Romania's National Agency for Cadastre and Land Registration (ANCPI), which continues to slow the completion of real estate transactions, North Bucharest Investments' latest analysis shows that demand across the residential market remains strong. World.title: Bucharest Community Foundation and City Hall begin transforming Herăstrău Park through public-private collaboration
World.content:
Bucharest City Hall and the Bucharest Community Foundation announced on Friday, July 31, that they have begun transforming the city’s major northern park, Herăstrău, according to the priorities expressed by nearly 10,000 participants in the public consultation.

The process benefits from private funding worth EUR 900,000 already mobilized by the Bucharest Community Foundation. The first EUR 90,000 will be invested in the studies and expertise required for the regeneration of the park’s green spaces, with the remainder to be directed as the stages are established together with the public administration.

The funds will cover the tree inventory through a TreePlotter-type digital application, the creation of a public inventory, specialized studies, technical and dendrological expertise, assessment of tree health and risk, preparation of the tree management plan, as well as the documentation needed to establish design requirements for future interventions.

The digital tree inventory will be public and accessible both to the administration and citizens and will form the basis of a Green Register dedicated to Old Herăstrău Park. For each tree, GIS location, dendrometric characteristics, health status, and management recommendations will be recorded. Data can be permanently updated by the public administration, and the tool can be gradually expanded to the entire Herăstrău Park, providing a permanent instrument for monitoring and adaptive and sustainable management of tree heritage.

The two partners began working together through a new collaboration model that brings together public administration, the community, specialists and private funders. The new working mechanism allows preparatory stages to begin quickly, independently of the public budget calendar, while maintaining decision-making, control and ownership of the documentation within the public administration.

The Bucharest Community Foundation will finance and contract specialists for the regeneration of green spaces based on specifications agreed with the authorities and experts involved, while the results will be handed over to the Bucharest City Hall and will serve as the basis for future design and construction works.

Meanwhile, the two partners will prepare the administrative framework for major interventions and mobilize the private sector and civil society to attract the financial resources necessary for the subsequent stages of the regeneration process. Private resources will accelerate project preparation without transferring decision-making rights over the park to funders. Control, validation and ownership of documentation will remain the responsibility of the public administration, while intervention solutions and priorities will be defined in collaboration with specialists, funders and community members, in accordance with the principles of the New European Bauhaus.

Going forward, the Bucharest Community Foundation aims to attract funds of up to EUR 10 million from the private sector and civil society for the subsequent intervention plan.

“If we waited for the completion of administrative procedures for landscape design, as well as for securing the lakeside area, we would not have enough speed. That is why I cannot sufficiently emphasize the role of the Bucharest Community Foundation. My role was to be open to collaboration and, together, to create this mechanism through which we can get on track, set things in motion, and accelerate interventions,” said Bucharest mayor Ciprian Ciucu.

Public consultation

The planned works follow a public consultation carried out between May and June 2026, in which nearly half of respondents said that they were dissatisfied with the current state of the park.

Participants’ expectations were very concrete. Modernization of general infrastructure was considered a priority by 83.2% of respondents, while 74.3% indicated the restoration of the natural environment as one of the main intervention directions. Permanent public toilets, more numerous and cleaner, represented the most requested specific measure resulting from the consultation, indicated by 85.5% of respondents. Better lighting at night was desired by 81.4% of respondents, followed by the rehabilitation of paths and paving (77.9%), ensuring functional drinking fountains (68.9%) and improving urban furniture (61.6%).

Restoring the natural environment was equally important. Among the respondents, 78.6% requested more trees and denser vegetation for shade, cooling and air filtration, while 71.2% wanted improved lake water quality, and 56.9% wanted better access to the waterfront. Nearly half of participants mentioned degraded paths and sidewalks among the main complaints, while responses indicate a clear preference for preserving the park’s natural character and avoiding excessive interventions.

World.title: Over 6 in 10 Romanians cannot afford a one-week annual vacation
World.content:
Romania ranks first in the European Union in terms of the share of people who cannot afford a one-week annual vacation away from home, according to data published by Eurostat on Thursday, July 30.

According to the European Statistical Office, 61.4% of Romanians aged 16 or older said they could not afford a one-week vacation away from home in 2025. Romania is followed by Greece, where 46.6% of residents were in the same situation, and by Bulgaria and Hungary, both with 39.1%.

The difference from the European Union average is significant. Across the 27 member states, 27.5% of people aged over 16 said they could not afford a one-week holiday away from home.

Compared with 2024, the share of people who cannot afford a vacation increased by 0.5% across the European Union. However, the long-term trend remains positive. Compared with 2015, the indicator has fallen by 7.7%, so over the last decade more and more Europeans have gained the financial ability to go on holiday for at least one week a year.

At the other end of the ranking are the states where an annual vacation is accessible to the vast majority of the population. The lowest share of people unable to afford a one-week holiday was recorded in Luxembourg, where only 10.6% of residents said they could not cover such an expense. It is followed by Sweden, with 12.4%, and the Netherlands, with 12.8%, values almost five times lower than those reported in Romania.

The ability to spend at least one week a year on vacation away from home is one of the indicators used by Eurostat to assess living conditions and the level of material deprivation in the member states. The data highlight the persistent differences between European economies in terms of purchasing power and households’ ability to cover expenses considered normal for a decent standard of living.
