World.title: No Dylans, no worries: Ponga pandemonium buries Broncos as a new star emerges
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 No Dylans, no worries: Ponga pandemonium buries Broncos as a new star emerges Nick Wright August 1, 2026 — 10:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Deprived of their superstar Dylans and with their season teetering, Kalyn Ponga issued a reminder to the NRL that the Knights were far from a spent force as long as he remained in the action. The Newcastle skipper proved a Suncorp Stadium menace, often leaving the Brisbane Broncos defence clutching at him in desperation as he orchestrated a 30-6 triumph to keep them embedded in the top eight. Reece Walsh of the Broncos takes on the defence of Kalyn Ponga of the Knights at Suncorp Stadium on Saturday Getty Images Ponga’s first-half exploits were enough to signal his intent – producing a pair of linebreak assists while also shrugging off a tackle and firing a pass for Dom Young to score as the Knights took a 14-0 half-time lead. It was an opening stanza which left the Broncos pondering which footy gods they angered as Adam Reynolds (concussion) and Xavier Willison (leg gnash) missed most of the match, and Deine Mariner and Reece Walsh were both sent to the sin bin.



Both Broncos’ sin binnings were contentious – Mariner deemed to have pulled Jermaine McEwen off an attacking chance, while Walsh was pinned for a hair pull on Young after joining a fight McEwen (also sent for 10 minutes) added fuel to as an unnecessary instigator. When Ponga wasn’t terrorising the Brisbane defence, his remaining attacking linchpin Fletcher Sharpe was doing all he could to offset the season-ending injury losses of Dylan Brown and Dylan Lucas. Related Article NRL 2026 Watch: The costly moments that sealed Broncos fate, and how they can avenge freefall It took less than three minutes for Sharpe to shrug off three defenders and open the scoring with the scything run, before going on to finish with 168 running metres and two linebreaks, before he pounced on a loose ball and scoring his second to close out the contest. The Broncos were left to rue a slew of wasted opportunities – a dropped pass by Josiah Karapani with the line in sight the most obvious in the first half, while Ben Hunt’s forward pass early in the second term for Kotoni Staggs to barge across also deemed forward.



Only a few minutes later, a Walsh cutout pass for Grant Anderson gave them another opportunity, only for the latter to be pushed into touch by Greg Marzhew before being able to ground the ball. From the very next set, a break from Young down the right-hand touchline ended up in Ponga’s hands, with the Queensland Maroons No.1 finding an offload for Phoenix Crossland to score. Payne Haas of the Broncos in action in the round 22 clash. Getty Images Brisbane stayed in the fight through some Walsh magic – the marquee man jumping into dummy-half and helping unleash Mariner, before the star fullback gathered the kick ahead to score. But a dropped ball from Mariner coming out of trouble sealed their fate – a brilliant put down in the corner from Marzhew after a Bradman Best flick pass ending any hopes of a Broncos’ comeback.



The win keeps the Knights just one win shy of the top four, with a bye still to come in round 27. A new star emerges Remember the name: Francis Manuleleua. Newcastle appears to have unearthed one of rugby league’s most promising young forwards, with the 22-year-old backrower producing a miracle pass and showcase of physicality to put his name in lights. One week on from what was a breakout performance from the rising star – in which he scored, set up a try and made two linebreaks in a one-point loss to the Roosters – Manuleleau ensured he would remain on pundits’ lips on the Knights’ run to the finals.



His 100 running metres and 31 tackles said enough. But it was an instinctive and ridiculous 20-metre cutout pass during broken play for Marzhew to cross in the corner that will be replayed in highlight reels for the rest of the season. His tackle in the shadows of half-time on Pat Carrigan, forcing a knock on with his pressure from the inside as the Broncos went on the attack one last time, was another sign of the potential eight-game Kiwi prospect possessed. While the loss of Lucas to a serious ankle injury has been a dagger-blow to the Knights’ top four hopes, Manuleleua, has presented enough hope to the Newcastle faithful that they had an X-factor in their pack to challenge the best of the competition. What’s left for Broncos to salvage? Has the time come for Broncos coach Michael Maguire to begin planning for season 2027?



Brisbane will welcome a quartet of recruits next year – Jonah Pezet, Mitch Barnett, Shawn Blore and Knights rival Dane Gagai all joining the Red Hill rebuild. But after Willison was forced from the action within six minutes, the lack of depth through the middle was made glaringly clear. Payne Haas, who will join South Sydney from next season, was easily the most dangerous forward for Brisbane with 111 running metres, although the unheralded Jaiyden Hunt (143 metres) punched above his weight. The medical retirement of Corey Jensen – who suffered a pulmonary embolism – has left the club without the same front-row partnership that delivered premiership glory in 2025. Rookie enforcer VJ Semu played the most minutes of his fledgling NRL career – running for 50 metres and making 33 tackles from 39 minutes. He needs to keep being exposed to this level to put him in the best position possible to make use of his 110kg frame regularly next year. Reynolds’ category one concussion ruling will keep him out of next week’s Battle of Brisbane against the Dolphins. That will likely thrust Tom Duffy into the fray, and there is an argument he should be given the rest of the campaign to prove he is the long-term successor to the retiring champion. Brisbane’s ruck manipulation has also been lacking in 2026, but looked far more potent when Billy Walters – in his second NRL game back from a ruptured ACL – was thrown into the action. He was denied a try assist by a Ben Talty knock on, and has been tipped to ink a contract extension. Whatever decision Maguire makes, it has gotten to a stage where forward-planning must be a priority.

World.title: What’s a museum if it returns all the loot: stony broke?
World.content:
I am not sure why it is called the British Museum in London, as it seems to mostly contain stuff the British stole (“Marbles return could set precedent”, July 26). Peter FitzSimons makes it clear in his chat with David Hill that the Parthenon Marbles ripped from the Parthenon in Athens with the compliance of the occupying Ottomans should be returned to Greece. When I was at the museum, I passed by many stolen treasures (booty?), and went down to see the amazing number of beautiful items from Benin, a country in Africa about which I did not know. It seems to have been a particularly brutal incursion. But then again, if the Brits did give back all the stuff they stole, what would they have left? Maybe bits of Stonehenge? Nola Tucker, Kiama

The Elgin Marbles: whose treasures should they be? Alamy Stock Photo

Hanson verbals single mums

Congratulations, Jacqueline Maley, on your dismantling of Pauline Hanson’s hateful non facts (“Forget crypto: single motherhood is Pauline’s get-rich-quick scheme”, July 25). My mother struggled to raise my sister and me from the 1940s. There was a stigma attached to divorced mothers, and she worried every day that our remarried father would claim custody of us. She was never allowed time off to attend our school functions. Sickness before Medicare was disastrous. She remarried badly, so she too could show a “respectable happy family”, and never had the wherewithal to escape that marriage. Mum never made it into the Senate, but she would never have spouted the sickening nonsense we hear from Pauline. Lynne Poleson, Kingsford

Pauline Hanson’s dismissal of the struggles faced by single mothers is hard to comprehend. Calling their situation a kind of “lottery” trivialises the reality: most women raising children alone do so under enormous pressure, not luck. The fact is that many women endure financial hardship, emotional strain, physical stress and constant fear. Collateral damage is their children, who may not be able to express but feel the stress of abuse. This isn’t the right place for political point-scoring. It’s a serious social issue involving real people who suffer because of coercive control, physical abuse and ongoing threats from ex-partners. Reducing that to a throwaway line is not just insensitive; it ignores the experience of thousands of families. This is an objectionable way of attracting manosphere MAGAs in Australia. The last thing we need is to throw away the progress made in making society a better and safer place, particularly for women and children. Mukul Desai, Hunters Hill

World.title: Carroll declares integrity a non-negotiable – and defends his own
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Carroll declares integrity a non-negotiable – and defends his own Chip Le Grand August 2, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The state’s peak anti-corruption agency will be given a broader remit as soon as possible to stamp out public sector malfeasance, conflicts of interest and improper influence that falls short of criminal conduct, as new Premier Ben Carroll seeks to restore public trust in government. Carroll said he would immediately seek advice on whether proposed changes to IBAC’s jurisdiction due to come into force at the end of next year could be brought forward. “If we can bring it forward, I will,” he said. Ben Carroll on Sunday: “I want to be a premier that is listening, that hears the message and gets on with it.” Wayne Taylor He promised that a special prosecutor working in tandem with a royal commission into the building industry to secure criminal convictions would be given whatever time and resources they need to clean up the corruption-plagued major projects sector. “I’m going to lead with integrity,” Carroll said. “Integrity is non-negotiable. It’s fundamental.



“I’m hoping the public will at least see that I’m trying to do the right thing by them.” Opposition Leader Jess Wilson released on Saturday her proposed terms of reference for a royal commission and a suggested list of witnesses including Daniel Andrews, Jacinta Allan and Carroll. Related Article Exclusive

Construction royal commission Bombshell briefing reveals top officials’ CFMEU warning to Allan Carroll said the terms of reference would be finalised this week and he had a shortlist of candidates for the roles of commissioner and special prosecutor. In seeking to explain the events that led up to last week’s dramatic change of Labor leader and premier, Carroll also addressed questions about his personal integrity.



He insists that he remained a loyal deputy to Allan until last Monday, when a delegation of cross-factional leaders told the former premier she had lost the support of her own government and urged Carroll to challenge for the leadership. It is less clear whether, as deputy premier, he made the case inside government for a royal commission or more urgent Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission reforms – steps he now says are crucial to restoring public faith in a 12-year-old Labor government. Related Article Visual Story

Construction royal commission Slow, then fast: The downfall of a premier under siege Two cabinet ministers have told The Age – and Carroll did not deny – that last Tuesday’s fateful caucus meeting was the first time he advocated for a royal commission into Big Build corruption in any government forum. When pressed on whether he counselled Allan privately to establish a royal commission, Carroll did not answer directly but said it was clear the former premier was not for turning.



“I didn’t raise things where it looked like the deputy and premier were on different sides of the fence,” he told The Age in an exclusive interview. “I raised with the premier a number of times that she needed to do something. Privately, I have also been talking to colleagues about a royal commission. “We spoke most Sunday nights before every cabinet meeting. She was very clear with her views and always sought my support. The role of the deputy is to give the premier support. Even when I disagreed with her privately, I’ve always backed her publicly and in the cabinet room. “The premier has known I have been wanting transparency and accountability for a long time.”



The comments are unlikely to heal the internal party wounds created by last week’s bruising leadership change. In a wide-ranging interview, Carroll revealed other instances where he disagreed with government decisions but was unable to publicly ventilate his concerns while upholding cabinet solidarity. Carroll admitted for the first time that a secret decision taken by the Allan government to delay by three years its commitment to fully fund public schools was a $2.4 billion funding cut and the wrong thing to do. The decision, which was exposed by The Age, is at the heart of the bitter wage dispute between the government and teachers. It was taken by the government’s budget and finance committee, of which the premier and deputy premier are members. Carroll, who is also education minister, opposed the move but failed to stop it. “I argued ferociously in the cabinet subcommittee process,” Carroll said. “I did speak up about it.” He said cabinet confidentially prevented him from publicly discussing the funding cut, even after it was revealed by this newspaper.



“When cabinet arrives at a position you need to support that position.” Carroll said the current pay offer before teachers, while generous, was not enough to fully fund government schools under the Gonski formula. He raised with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last week the need to lift school funding in Victoria and deliver the long-awaited Gonski reforms. Related Article Opinion

School funding In the so-called education state, Gonski puts our schools stone-cold last Chip Le Grand State political editor “I am committed to try and get full and fair funding for our public schools,” he said. He agreed the tax burden on business in Victoria, particularly since increases to payroll tax and land tax announced by former treasurer Tim Pallas in 2023, needed to be lightened. The tax rises were announced as temporary but are due to remain in force until 2033.



“We want to be competitive with NSW. We’ve got to do everything we can to make it easy to start a business in Victoria and grow a business,” Carroll said. “We’ve also just got to support everyday Victorians who are working hard every day. We are in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis which is hurting and biting and it has no end in sight.” One of the 2023 tax increases removed the payroll tax exemption for non-government schools. While the impost was adjusted in this year’s budget to impact fewer schools, Carroll left open the possibility of scrapping it altogether. “I think this was a necessary measure for the time, but I’m always open to continue working with the sector,” he said. Carroll said the planned Suburban Rail Loop, the most expensive infrastructure project in the state’s history, was a good concept undermined by the way it was developed, in secret, under then-premier Daniel Andrews in the lead-up to the 2018 election.



While the government’s contractual commitments to the SRL and the project’s financial assumptions will be reviewed by cabinet, Carroll said the rail line already under construction needed to be built. Related Article Victorian Parliament Down to business: Carroll leaves door open to work-from-home changes “I have always believed the project is a great concept. The problem with the SRL is its gestation period – it never had one. Airport rail had been talked about for 100 years. SRL was never part of the public discussion. It came as a surprise to a lot of people, including cabinet members. “However, the project does have merit and the project does need to continue. I’m not going to stop contracts or rip up contracts. That era is over.” He acknowledged concerns expressed by Victoria’s integrity agencies about the budget squeeze on their operations and capacity to expose corruption, misconduct and financial mismanagement.



“We need strong, independent agencies – IBAC, the Auditor-General, the Ombudsman. We are stewards of our public finances and institutions. That’s a role I take very seriously.” When asked about reports that he wants to change legislation, currently before parliament, to give people a legal right to work from home two days a week, Carroll said the government would consider sensible amendments but not move any itself. Loading Since taking the leadership, he has been repeatedly questioned and attacked by the opposition over comments he made six weeks ago, referencing his daughter, in which he vowed to support Jacinta Allan through to the state election. He said it was not the first time he had made the comment and that he previously wrote to Allan expressing the same sentiment.



Related Article Analysis

Victorian election The hatred of Jacinta Allan was unfair. But it had become visceral Carroll and Allan had a private meeting in the premier’s office the day before Tuesday’s leadership spill. Neither has disclosed what was discussed. Carroll said that by then, the political reality had changed, with an unrelenting corruption scandal cruelling whatever chance Allan and Labor had to remain in power after the November 28 state election. “We’d all been out door-knocking and it was very clear we weren’t getting the message through,” he said. Instead, voters were outraged at the estimated $15 billion cost of the Building Bad scandal documented by this masthead. “I want to be a premier that is listening, that hears the message and gets on with it. That’s why my first act was to call the royal commission. It’s why I will give the police commissioner every power and resource he needs. It’s why I will do what I can do to give IBAC the power and resources it needs. “And then, there are things I want to do that are part of Labor’s DNA.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Our regular quizmaster is excited to put your general knowledge to the test with a new set of 15 crafty questions every day.



Can I see the number of questions in the quiz? Yes, the total number of questions is displayed next to the progress bar at the top of the quiz. The number of your current question is also shown (e.g. 3/15). Want to keep track of your score? You can find a running tally in green at the top right of the quiz. Can I see all the quiz questions at a glance? No, we challenge players to complete the quiz one question at a time.



When I answer a question, there’s a percentage next to the correct and incorrect answers. Why? Thanks for noticing! This is a new addition to the quiz. It lets you track how your score compares to other readers by showing the percentage of players who chose that particular answer. It will also help you gauge the difficulty of each question after you’ve answered. Can I reset the quiz for other players on my device? Yes, click or tap ‘Play Again’ at the end of the results screen to reset the quiz.

World.title: No Dylans, no worries: Ponga pandemonium buries Broncos as a new star emerges
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 No Dylans, no worries: Ponga pandemonium buries Broncos as a new star emerges Nick Wright August 1, 2026 — 10:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Deprived of their superstar Dylans and with their season teetering, Kalyn Ponga issued a reminder to the NRL that the Knights were far from a spent force as long as he remained in the action. The Newcastle skipper proved a Suncorp Stadium menace, often leaving the Brisbane Broncos defence clutching at him in desperation as he orchestrated a 30-6 triumph to keep them embedded in the top eight. Reece Walsh of the Broncos takes on the defence of Kalyn Ponga of the Knights at Suncorp Stadium on Saturday Getty Images Ponga’s first-half exploits were enough to signal his intent – producing a pair of linebreak assists while also shrugging off a tackle and firing a pass for Dom Young to score as the Knights took a 14-0 half-time lead. It was an opening stanza which left the Broncos pondering which footy gods they angered as Adam Reynolds (concussion) and Xavier Willison (leg gnash) missed most of the match, and Deine Mariner and Reece Walsh were both sent to the sin bin.



Both Broncos’ sin binnings were contentious – Mariner deemed to have pulled Jermaine McEwen off an attacking chance, while Walsh was pinned for a hair pull on Young after joining a fight McEwen (also sent for 10 minutes) added fuel to as an unnecessary instigator. When Ponga wasn’t terrorising the Brisbane defence, his remaining attacking linchpin Fletcher Sharpe was doing all he could to offset the season-ending injury losses of Dylan Brown and Dylan Lucas. Related Article NRL 2026 Watch: The costly moments that sealed Broncos fate, and how they can avenge freefall It took less than three minutes for Sharpe to shrug off three defenders and open the scoring with the scything run, before going on to finish with 168 running metres and two linebreaks, before he pounced on a loose ball and scoring his second to close out the contest. The Broncos were left to rue a slew of wasted opportunities – a dropped pass by Josiah Karapani with the line in sight the most obvious in the first half, while Ben Hunt’s forward pass early in the second term for Kotoni Staggs to barge across also deemed forward.



Only a few minutes later, a Walsh cutout pass for Grant Anderson gave them another opportunity, only for the latter to be pushed into touch by Greg Marzhew before being able to ground the ball. From the very next set, a break from Young down the right-hand touchline ended up in Ponga’s hands, with the Queensland Maroons No.1 finding an offload for Phoenix Crossland to score. Payne Haas of the Broncos in action in the round 22 clash. Getty Images Brisbane stayed in the fight through some Walsh magic – the marquee man jumping into dummy-half and helping unleash Mariner, before the star fullback gathered the kick ahead to score. But a dropped ball from Mariner coming out of trouble sealed their fate – a brilliant put down in the corner from Marzhew after a Bradman Best flick pass ending any hopes of a Broncos’ comeback.



The win keeps the Knights just one win shy of the top four, with a bye still to come in round 27. A new star emerges Remember the name: Francis Manuleleua. Newcastle appears to have unearthed one of rugby league’s most promising young forwards, with the 22-year-old backrower producing a miracle pass and showcase of physicality to put his name in lights. One week on from what was a breakout performance from the rising star – in which he scored, set up a try and made two linebreaks in a one-point loss to the Roosters – Manuleleau ensured he would remain on pundits’ lips on the Knights’ run to the finals.



His 100 running metres and 31 tackles said enough. But it was an instinctive and ridiculous 20-metre cutout pass during broken play for Marzhew to cross in the corner that will be replayed in highlight reels for the rest of the season. His tackle in the shadows of half-time on Pat Carrigan, forcing a knock on with his pressure from the inside as the Broncos went on the attack one last time, was another sign of the potential eight-game Kiwi prospect possessed. While the loss of Lucas to a serious ankle injury has been a dagger-blow to the Knights’ top four hopes, Manuleleua, has presented enough hope to the Newcastle faithful that they had an X-factor in their pack to challenge the best of the competition. What’s left for Broncos to salvage? Has the time come for Broncos coach Michael Maguire to begin planning for season 2027?



Brisbane will welcome a quartet of recruits next year – Jonah Pezet, Mitch Barnett, Shawn Blore and Knights rival Dane Gagai all joining the Red Hill rebuild. But after Willison was forced from the action within six minutes, the lack of depth through the middle was made glaringly clear. Payne Haas, who will join South Sydney from next season, was easily the most dangerous forward for Brisbane with 111 running metres, although the unheralded Jaiyden Hunt (143 metres) punched above his weight. The medical retirement of Corey Jensen – who suffered a pulmonary embolism – has left the club without the same front-row partnership that delivered premiership glory in 2025. Rookie enforcer VJ Semu played the most minutes of his fledgling NRL career – running for 50 metres and making 33 tackles from 39 minutes. He needs to keep being exposed to this level to put him in the best position possible to make use of his 110kg frame regularly next year. Reynolds’ category one concussion ruling will keep him out of next week’s Battle of Brisbane against the Dolphins. That will likely thrust Tom Duffy into the fray, and there is an argument he should be given the rest of the campaign to prove he is the long-term successor to the retiring champion. Brisbane’s ruck manipulation has also been lacking in 2026, but looked far more potent when Billy Walters – in his second NRL game back from a ruptured ACL – was thrown into the action. He was denied a try assist by a Ben Talty knock on, and has been tipped to ink a contract extension. Whatever decision Maguire makes, it has gotten to a stage where forward-planning must be a priority.

World.title: European fires bring into focus climate emergency
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters European fires bring into focus climate emergency August 1, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Climate work crisis

Your correspondent (Letters, 31/7) answers her own question on the Bordeaux fires. Should we recognise the more frequent disasters like this, or risk hitting the tourism industry?

Of course, the world needs to acknowledge the direct link of extreme weather to fossil fuels burning.

People and governments have been complacent for many reasons. Problems like cost of living take precedence when results are wanted by the next election.

Individual floods and droughts are complex, not caused by global warming alone. Australia has always been a land “of droughts and flooding rains”.

But these are excuses, demolished for years by science, and recently by unprecedented fires in places like Bordeaux.

More needs to be done now to reduce the even worse impacts that will come in the second half of this century.

John Hughes, Mentone AI as a subject

Kylie Moore-Gilbert (Comment, 30/7) expresses deep concerns about the use of AI in high schools, worrying that children whose brains are still developing will become deskilled in thinking for themselves. I recognise these concerns, but wonder whether it is possible to safely and proactively equip students to responsibly use AI by focusing on process more than outcome. Prompts are key to AI use. Students could start by looking at a question from numerous angles to elicit a large number of prompts, explaining their reasoning along the way. No one achieves a final draft immediately, so students could submit their drafts as well with their own evaluation of them. Hopefully, by incorporating AI as a compulsory subject in the curriculum, the next gen – ″⁣AI natives″⁣ – will have the knowledge and understanding to ethically, creatively and confidently function in an uncertain future.

Sue Fisher, Coburg A depressendon thought

Depressendon–- couldn’t have picked a better word, Kate Halfpenny (Comment, 01/8). If James Hird gets another crack after two previous failed attempts, I’m out, too. Will make it to the Fitzroy ground and barrack for the Royboys in the amateur league. Maybe that’s where the Bombers should be.

Moira Macdonald, Daylesford



Outsourcing to the client

Waleed Aly has hit the nail on the head (Comment, 31/7). One wonders sometimes, how some people manage tasks that used to be so straightforward. The reality is that businesses have, in effect, outsourced to us what used to be their service offering or obligation. We now do the work, carry the risk, do the waiting and experience the frustrations while they claim ″⁣efficiency″⁣! The organisation that comes up with a better ″⁣digital solution″⁣ will be a winner.

Charles Griss, Balwyn Learn the new ways

Remember the abacus and ″⁣log books″⁣ of logarithmic and trigonometric functions? In the ’70s, my mentor began teaching me how to repair three-legged transistors, diodes, resistors and some capacitors operating as a four function 20kg lump of desktop calculator.

Decades later, I lifted the lid on an Intel Pentium microprocessor and with a decent microscope you could probe a subminiature world for two etched signatures left by the ″⁣artwork″⁣ engineers. Presumably there are still people who understand how (now) billions of transistors connect and operate in modern devices.

A friend is trying to guide me through the mathematics of crude image recognition AI. It troubles me that few people understand or care how anything actually works in our brave new world.

Ronald Elliott, Sandringham City needs the SRL

Melbourne 2050 – population nine million. Hundreds of thousands of more cars on the streets. Gridlock wherever you go. Why didn’t we build the SRL, like every other major world city which has one? It’s there for generations to come.

George Djoneff, Mitcham Longer vision needed

The SRL is a perfect example of the moral and political dilemmas those politicians with a long-term vision always face (“Carroll considers rail loop’s future”, 30/7).

There will always be a choice between spending money to benefit future generations and the immediate needs of the voters, especially in health, education, and housing. The benefits of the SRL will not be felt until there is appropriate supporting development and people start to see the need to rely on public transport far more than we currently do.

When we say we should leave the world in good condition for future generations, most people are thinking about their children, grandchildren and maybe even their great grandchildren, when inreality we should be thinking more like Indigenous peoples around the world.

They think about the impact of their behaviour on the next seven generations or beyond. As current representatives of humanity, we are far too self-focused.

There was much ongoing opposition to London’s underground rail system when it was first proposed in the mid-19th century.

Howard Tankey, Box Hill North Widen commission

At best, SRL East would rank at the bottom of a top 10 priority strategic infrastructure projects list, if the best interests of all Victorians were considered, not least jobs, economic productivity and air quality for the western suburbs and growth corridor to Geelong and beyond.

With news of yet more cost blow-outs on this project too, this project should also come within the purview of the royal commission, along with all these dubious planning approvals for excessive height and site coverage around train stations.

There’s no reason Melbourne has to become a mega city of highrise towers leaving no room for sunshine and trees, certainly not if it means trashing liveability, so the question remains, who benefits?

Bernadette George, Mildura



Recall Kennett years

Your correspondent (Letters, 31/7) confidently suggests that “the Liberals would never be so reckless with taxpayer money” as they imply Labor has been. We might also reflect on the short-term budget gains over long-term public value of the privatisations and public sector restructures prioritised by the Kennett Liberal government (1992-99).

Bruce Watson, Clifton Springs Weighing the risks

Cartoonist Cathy Wilcox (1/8) has captured the irony of modern technology by showing how ludicrous it is to use a valuable resource to cool down data centres and the risk of more wildfires? What is the balance between supporting these digital services that rely on water and the use of a resource that is essential for people, agriculture and the environment?

Julie Ottobre, Brunswick East The pleasure of trees

Like columnist Melissa Hoyer (Comment, 30/7) I find it extremely sad when mature trees are cut down, whatever the reason given – the beautiful mature peppercorn trees near the tennis courts next to the council gym in Gleadell Street, Richmond, for example.

I’ve been going to the gym for nearly 40 years and I’ve always passed those trees with a feeling of intense pleasure at the sight of them: they’ve provided deep shade and beauty to generations of tennis players and passers-by, and heaven knows we need them in such a heavily concreted area.

Bill Mack, Kew The bee all and end all?

With the escalation of climate difficulties being so vivid across the planet, how are bees fairing?

Richard Pentony, Hawthorn

World.title: NPC: Mo'unga scores match-winning try for Canterbury against Auckland
World.content:
Richie Mo'unga has scored the winning try for Canterbury in his first NPC match since 2020, with the defending champions beating Auckland 38-31.

Mo'unga, who has spent the last three years playing in Japan, came on as a replacement in the second half on Saturday night, and while he had a few awkward moments, he turned on the class to split the Auckland defence in the 78th minute, when the scores were deadlocked.

The first half was helter-skelter, with Canterbury starting off where they left off last season, with early dominance at the breakdown seeing them score two tries in the first 11 minutes.

But Auckland stormed back when the red-and-blacks made a couple of errors, leaving a hole in their lineout for Sam Hainsworth-Fa'aofo to score and then gifting an intercept to Xavier Tito-Harris.

Canterbury then scored two more tries, but Auckland claimed one back to trail 26-21 at halftime.

There was a big cheer when Mo'unga took the field but he looked a bit rusty early, knocking forward a ball that bounced just in front of him and then missing a conversion he normally would have nailed.

Auckland had taken the lead for the first time in the 60th minute, but Canterbury hit back seven minutes later.

It was 31-all with 12 minutes to go and stayed that way, until Canterbury's forwards charged towards the Auckland line from a lineout after winning a penalty and Mo'unga got his hands on the ball playing halfback, fooling the defence with a dummy and scoring by the posts. He then converted it.

In earlier games today, Otago beat Southland 41-14, and Taranaki beat Counties Manukau 20 points to five.

On Friday night, Tasman pipped North Harbour 31-29 in Nelson, while Waikato opened the season with a 38-26 win over Bay of Plenty on Thursday.

World.title: Country Life: Hydroponics in Horowhenua
World.content:
There's no need for extra washing when it comes to these salad greens. The plants from Waikawa fresh are harvested straight from their trays where they're grown hydroponically.

"There's no bugs, there's no soil, there's no dirt. We don't clean these plants with any chemicals or chlorine, so we eat those lettuce straight out of the channels. They're just absolutely crispy clean ... and they haven't been touched by anyone the whole time it's been growing," Tony Dale-Low told Country Life.

He and wife Lisa Dale-Low made the move to growing salad greens and herbs almost a decade ago, trading in city life and corporate jobs for horticulture in Horowhenua.

Hydroponics in Horowhenua: Growing with water Country Life Download MP3 17m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

The couple had no growing experience before starting.

They'd spent a couple of years travelling around the country in a bus with their three children before coming up with a checklist of what they wanted for their next chapter.

"We wanted to be doing something productive, rather than something paper or computer-based. We wanted to be rural and we wanted to have a bit more flexibility with the kids. None of that was really sector specific or even location-specific," Lisa said.

The couple grow fancy lettuces and other herby greens hydroponically. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Hydroponic growing systems work by replacing soil with a water-based, nutrient-rich solution. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The water sourced from the 4500m2 of rooves of the many greenhouses, and the recent addition of solar power is also helping cut down on energy bills. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

After narrowing it down to the North Island they came across an existing hydroponic growing business near Levin - hydroponic systems work by replacing soil with a water-based, nutrient-rich solution.

That was in 2018 and after learning the ropes from the previous owners they've made it their own.

They grow the plants from seedlings themselves, also using hydroponics on a 'flood and drain table'.

"So this is set up on a timer. It runs three times a day and these tables will fill with nutrients or liquid with some fertilizer," Tony explained.

Seedlings, like these little basil sprouts, are also grown hydroponically. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The seedlings are easily plugged into the next growing space. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

It sits there for a few minutes before draining. Being fully automated means the team don't need to do any manual watering.

He said it helps the plants up well - making them more resistant to diseases and pests.

"[It] all definitely starts here in the propagating house. If we get it wrong here, then we have issues later. If we get it right, then we have so much more success."

Once the seedlings reach about three weeks, they're transferred to larger growing trays called 'gullies'.

"They look like downpipes, which in fact I think they are, actually straight off someone's house," Tony told Country Life.

"They've been drilled with a lot of little round holes and we plant the plant inside the holes. The nutrients get pumped around the greenhouse through these small whiskers."

Among some of the 'fancy' lettuces they grow, the oak leaf in red and green varieties. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The couple learned the art of hydroponics from the previous owners. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Over the cooler winter months, it gets too cold to grow basil so they replace this with growing watercress instead. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The system they use only requires liquid to be pumped to the top of the gully before gravity does the rest, drawing it down the channel, through the gutter back to the holding tank which is topped up with the water sourced from the 4500m2 of greenhouse rooves.

The water is reticulated meaning they only need to add more to account for evaporation or absorption by the plants.

In the central tank, a computer system checks to make sure the water has the right balance of nutrients and the right pH level - the acid or alkaline concentration - and runs a dosing system to adjust this when needed.

Tony and his green 'lettuce' Leaf - the old Nissan Leaf gets its power from solar panels on the farm and is used to run around the property for the many maintenance jobs. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Sustainability is a key part of Waikawa Fresh' operations.

The recent addition of solar power at the end of last year is also helping cut down on energy bills - it's even used to power an old Nissan 'lettuce' leaf they use on farm to run the maintenance gear around.

About two months after the plants have finished growing they'll be ready to be picked straight from the gullies with no extra washing required - "lovely and crunchy and and fresh".

From their hands where they're packed straight into bags, the harvested plants are taken straight to the chiller ready to be picked up by a truck that same day. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Getting the product to the market as fresh as possible is a key focus. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

World.title: Four in custody after staff assaulted, haul of perfume taken, police say
World.content:
Police responding to a report of a perfume heist say they quickly were able to quickly "sniff out" the leads and detain four young people.

Just before 2pm on Saturday, Hamilton police were called to a report that staff at a store at The Base shopping centre "had been assaulted and thousands of dollars' worth of perfume had been taken," a Police bulletin said.

"No weapons were used, nor were there any injuries."

Senior Sergeant Pete Simpson said officers who responded were given details about the possible identity of the suspects, and video captured by a person at the scene.

By 2:25pm on Saturday, officers had found "a bag full of the stolen items" at a nearby address, Simpson said.

Four young people were taken into custody, and are expected to appear in court on robbery charges next week.

World.title: Two new Auckland stations part of $2.4b rail spend
World.content:
Two new railway stations in South Auckland are among the final elements of a $2.4 billion government investment in Auckland's network, Minister for Auckland Simon Watts says.

He was speaking at the formal opening on Saturday of the Drury and Paerātā stops.

The stations will serve Drury, Paerātā, Franklin and South Auckland, with each station providing two platforms, 350 car parks and bus connections.

Services begin stopping at the new stations on Sunday. During the week, peak trains will run every 10 minutes.

Rail Minister Winston Peters at the opening of the new Drury station. RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

Other speakers at the opening were Rail Minister Winston Peters, KiwiRail chief metro officer Bevan Assink and Franklin ward councillor Andy Baker.

Watts said that while much of the recent investment in the rail network had been about preparing for the opening of the CRL, "the extension of the overhead electrification from Papakura to Pukekohe and these new train stations represent something more".

"Trains stopping at Drury and Paerātā stations from tomorrow and Ngākōroa station when it opens next year will help open up this part of Auckland.

"Around 130,000 more people are expected to be in the southern part of Auckland over the next three decades. More than 40,000 new homes are expected to be built, a new hospital in Drury, a number of new schools, new roads, including in time the Mill Road extension.

"For locals, it means ... being part of an Auckland that is properly connected to the rest of the city... It will give people greater confidence to move to this part of Auckland, knowing that they will not be reliant on their cars, and overall it's a great choice about where people live and how they get around," Watts said.

Auckland's new Paerātā railway station. RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

KiwiRail's Bevan Assink gave the gathering some project numbers - 6500 cubic metres of concrete; 600 tonnes of locally sourced steel; 25,000 cubic metres of material moved to make way for the facilities.

"We've also planted around 40,000 trees and everything to beautify the area. Also there were 22 apprenticeships that were able to be enacted as part of this project and also 32 local companies were also involved in the project as well.

"So it just shows how broad and vast-reaching these projects can be in supporting the communities and everything around them," Assink said.

Franklin ward's Andy Baker told a story of two girls, aged 11 and 12, writing to him in 2011 to ask if Drury could get a railway station.

"They had done a petition here in Drury. They had hundreds and hundreds of signatures about wanting a park and ride and a station at Drury.

"One of those girls is here today - my daughter ... she may have had some egging on ... the other, the 11-year-old at the time ... is now an emergency doctor at Christchurch Hospital, so time has moved on.

"I did promise Emma it would be built before she left high school, which was 2015, but we haven't quite made that.

"But it shows that there's been a demand for this type of infrastructure in this area for a very, very long time. It is fantastic to see it today," Baker said.

RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

Rail Minister Peters echoed Watts' figure of 130,000 more people expected in the area over coming decades "and infrastructure must come before growth - not years afterwards, as too often happens in this country".

"These stations are here because we funded them when last responsible for rail, as part of our wider commitments to unlock capacity, lift train frequencies, invest more than $500 million to get the network up to standard, and enable electric trains from Britomart right down to Pukekohe.

"While others say nice words about rail, we fund it, deliver it, and on this happy occasion are still here to open it.

"We will keep advocating for rail because taxpayers have built an asset with real potential to move people and goods efficiently - and we intend to make full use of it."

In an earlier statement, Transport Minister Chris Bishop said the stations were among the final elements of a $2.4 billion government investment in Auckland's rail network.

"The Auckland Rail Network Rebuild has been completed in time for the City Rail Link to open soon. We're also replacing level crossings across the network to support more frequent train services.

"The Third Main Line is now open, separating freight and passenger rail services, while the rail line to Pukekohe has been electrified. Looking ahead, new rail stations at Ngākōroa are also set to open in 2027.

The work was about investing in infrastructure "that would help our largest city to grow".

World.title: 5.2 magnitude quake strikes near Te Anau
World.content:
Te Anau has been hit by a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, just a week after being jolted by a 5.9.

The latest quake, at 3:23pm on Saturday, was centred 35 kilometres north-west of the town at a depth of 102 kilometres, GeoNet said.

Felt reports showed more than 1400 people felt the shaking, mostly in the lower South Island.

There were no immediate reports of damage.

On 25 July a magnitude 5.9 earthquake struck 40 kilometres north of Te Anau, sparking a brief tsunami warning and an evacuation notice for some areas of the West Coast, which was later cancelled.

On Friday night, a magnitude 4.6 quake jolted the lower North Island and upper South at 11:09pm. It was centred 30 kilometres offshore, north-west of Porirua at a depth of 38 kilometres, and more than 8900 people logged Felt Reports.

GeoNet scientist Jonathan Hanson said New Zealand has been living up to its Shaky Isles reputation. While it had been a busy few weeks in terms of earthquakes, overall it was not unusual.

There are typically 15 to 20 magnitude five events in the country every year, but having a couple approaching magnitude six in a month is less common.

"These deep earthquakes are typically widely felt," GeoNet wrote on Facebook on Saturday afternoon.

World.title: Rising shop violence demands stronger penalties: Retail NZ
World.content:
Retailers need stronger powers to protect staff and customers from violent repeat offenders, Retail NZ says, amid reports of rapidly escalating aggression.

The Justice Select Committee is recommending by majority that The Trespass Amendment Bill be passed into law.

The bill would give retailers the power to trespass people from multiple sites, double fines to $2000 and increase the maximum trespass period to three years.

Retail NZ chief executive Carolyn Young said violence in stores was on the rise, with people becoming more agitated and entering businesses with concealed weapons.

"They will come in with knives, with hammers, with screwdrivers, with machetes ... Some stores within their stores sell things that can be turned into a weapon ... People will come in to a hardware store and use things on their shelves to threaten staff to be able to steal goods or do harm to people," she said.

"We have also seen guns that have been presented in certain circumstances, and all of those things mean that it's not a safe environment for staff members or customers."

Young said clear guidance would be needed to ensure new powers were used appropriately.

'Not convinced' - Labour and Greens

Opposition parties have raised concerns about the proposed changes, while questioning if harsher penalties would work as an effective deterrent to retail crime.

Labour said that despite some improvements to the bill, it remained concerned about the proposed scope of multi-location trespass notices.

"We remain concerned that there will be situations when vulnerable individuals may be unable to access essential goods and services due to the scope of these notices.

"We are also not convinced that the increase in penalties will act as an effective deterrent and consider there are other policies that may more effectively address the drivers of crime," it said.

The Green Party said it did not support the bill and remained concerned that the increase in fines from $1000 to $2000 would be "unrealistic" for offenders, who often resorted to retail crime as a result of the cost-of-living crisis.

"It is important that we have the right balance between clarity for retail stores and safety of retail employees and owners. However, we do not believe this will result in the expected effect of deterrence for retail crime," it said.

World.title: Queenstown mayor wants ideas on relieving traffic snarls
World.content:
An influx of tourists is causing massive traffic problems across the Wakatipu Basin, the mayor of the Queenstown-Lakes District says.

The council was setting up a mayoral taskforce on reducing congestion, Mayor John Glover said.

"Our state highway networks are really struggling to cope at peak times ... we are seeing some significant gridlock.

"A drive that probably would have taken 10 minutes at times is taking 90 minutes," he said.

The gridlock was prompting complaints on social media. Those living in new housing developments were struggling to get on to the state highway as well.

"We actually need some traffic control to wave people through in the right places so that traffic can keep flowing," Glover said.

"Maybe a bit of human intervention to keep things going at some of these junctions might do the job."

World.title: Dozens of greyhounds to land in Australia as NZ racing ban begins
World.content:
Chartered flights will ferry up to 150 greyhounds to Australia as trainers pivot from a racing ban coming into effect in New Zealand.

The ban, which was first announced in December 2024 and legislated in April this year, took effect on Saturday after years of animal welfare concerns.

Ten greyhounds were euthanised during New Zealand's final racing season, including one days before the ban began.

Heather Simpson, the Greyhound Transition Agency (GTA) head, said she was aware that Greyhound Racing New Zealand had organised charter flights for about 150 dogs to go to Australia to continue racing.

"There is nothing in the legislation that stops trainers choosing to export their dogs to Australia; some of these dogs actually will be partly owned by Australians," she told Radio New Zealand.

Greyhound ban legislation delayed until government gets support A bill to ban greyhound racing in Tasmania has been delayed until the government can secure enough support.

Greyhound racing remains legal in most Australian jurisdictions, banned only in the Australian Capital Territory.

Plans for an industry phase-out in Tasmania have stalled after the government pulled a bill from the upper house in April when it appeared not to have enough support to pass.

Word of the chartered flights first emerged through a leaked message from a private greyhound racing group, Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi told a Senate Rural and Regional Affairs and Transport Legislation Committee hearing in April.

She said the move appeared "to be kind of a deliberate attempt to avoid" New Zealand's transition agency.

"If they survive, they will become the responsibility of Australians to rehome," she said.

"And you would know we're already in a rehoming crisis."

The greyhounds brought to Australia will be classed as "companion animals". (Reuters: Action Images/Scott Heavey)

Brant Smith, a senior biosecurity executive at the Department of Agriculture and Fisheries, told the senate hearing the government had been working with New Zealand's Ministry for Primary Industries on the dogs' import.

He said they would be classed as "companion animals", but may be used for racing once in the country.

"As to how they are then used, that's not something that we have control over thereafter because they're being imported as companion animals like other animals … and this is not unusual," he said.

Mr Smith said a similar contingent of greyhounds was imported to Australia in April 2025.

"In the previous consignment, I think approximately 80 came similarly, and they were just imported under our normal conditions," he said.

It is estimated a further 1,400 dogs will remain in New Zealand and require rehoming by the GTA.

Ms Simpson said the rehomed dogs would be regularly checked under a welfare program.

World.title: Broncos to 'look after each other' as title defence comes to early end
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos coach Michael Maguire has said the playing group will need to "look after each other" as their finals hopes were officially ended on Saturday night.

The Broncos will become the first reigning premier in 20 years to miss the finals after going down at home to the Newcastle Knights 30-6.

Brisbane has just six wins this season, in a premiership defence that has been hampered by injuries and poor performances.

With any faint hopes of making the finals ending with a 24-point loss to the Knights, Maguire told media the club would need to rally around each other in the face of a disappointing campaign.

"It is tough, because I've got a high regard on how these boys go about things," Maguire said.

"You can't fault how they try. Unfortunately at the moment, we're not getting things going our way.

"I feel for everyone that's going through it at the moment.

"But they're a group that support each other, and that's what it's about now.

"We've got to make sure that we look after each other through this period."

Brisbane becomes the first reigning premier to not make finals since Wests Tigers missed the top eight in 2006 after winning the grand final in 2005.

Earlier, Penrith winger Tom Jenkins has become the first player in 72 years to score multiple tries in 12 matches during a season, as the Panthers hammered the Canberra Raiders 42-18 in Mudgee.

The New Zealand Warriors consolidated their place in the NRL top four with a commanding win over the Gold Coast Titans.

Relive all of Saturday's NRL action in the blog below.

World.title: Fraser sheds light on coaching call as Blues record monster win over Lions
World.content:
Carlton's interim coach Josh Fraser says he will decide this week whether to join the club's process to find its next full-time coach.

Fraser's candidacy received another major boost as the Blues recorded a thumping 24.10 (154) to 11.12 (78) win over the Brisbane Lions at Docklands Stadium in club captain Patrick Cripps's 250th career game.

While Fraser began his coaching tenure by stating he wasn't interested in the full-time role, a stunning 9-2 record has caused him to reconsider his original position.

Carlton's win also enhanced its bid for a wildcard spot, with the Blues in 10th spot on the AFL ladder, four premiership points ahead of the ninth-placed St Kilda and the 10th-placed GWS Giants.

The Giants overcame a gritty Port Adelaide side to claim a 10.15 (75) to 9.9 (63) win at the Adelaide Oval to stay within touch of the final wildcard spot.

Earlier on Saturday, Sydney recorded a comeback 16.11 (107) to 13.10 (88) win against St Kilda at Docklands Stadium, but lost Will Edwards to a horror injury, with the result dealing a blow to the Saints' wildcard bid.

Meanwhile, Hawthorn survived a stiff test against North Melbourne before running out 14.15 (99) to 12.11 (83) winners in Tasmania.

In a curtain-raiser for the AFLW season, Australia recorded a 13.13 (91) to 6.5 (41) win against Ireland at North Sydney Oval as Jasmine Garner was named the Player of the Match.

Follow the live blog below for recap of all of Saturday's football action as it happened.

World.title: Boxer earns Tuvalu's first ever Comm Games medal without winning fight
World.content:
A boxer from Tuvalu earned her tiny South Pacific nation's first ever Commonwealth Games medal without winning a fight overnight.

Tarona Taafaki lost her only bout in the women's 75-kilogram class to India's Lovlina Borgohain, losing every round on all three of the judges' cards.

Because there were only five entrants, Taafaki received a bye to the last four, meaning she was automatically guaranteed at least a bronze medal.

Tarona Taafaki arrives at the Commonwealth Games during the opening ceremony. (AP: Kin Cheung)

But her coach and father said the population of Tuvalu, an island south-east of Tonga, will celebrate the medal and use it to highlight a climate change emergency.

Badi Taafaki, whose son Pasoni competed earlier in the Games and lost his only bout at 70kg, told the British Press Association: "For the people of Tuvalu, this medal means everything.

"We're one of the smallest nations in the world, so a medal like this is hugely significant. We have worked so hard to get here. For me as a coach, it's a stepping stone."

Tarona and Pasoni are the two eldest of eight children, all of whom are boxers. They are based in New Zealand in order to take advantage of better facilities.

"My children are very fortunate," Badi said.

"They have opportunities and facilities that I never had. Boxing is our whole life. Strength is in our bloodline."

Athletes on the island famously train on its airport runway, the most stable land mass on an island increasingly threatened by rising sea levels. Climate experts predict half of the nation's capital, Funafuti, could be submerged by 2050.

A group of locals play volleyball on the airport runway in Funafuti, Tuvalu. (Getty Images: Fiona Goodall)

"Yes, we train on the airport runway," Badi said. "When a plane comes in, everyone moves aside. As soon as it leaves, we go back on the tarmac, because there is nowhere else to train.

"If we can win medals, more people around the world will recognise Tuvalu and begin to understand the challenges we face because of climate change.

"It is very real for us. The coastal erosion is unbelievable, and the countdown is now measured in years, not decades. Some islands have lost half their land. At high tide the sea comes right through. People living on the coast can't sleep if there's a storm, because the waves can come straight through their homes."

Tarona is not the first boxer to win a Commonwealth Games medal without winning a fight. Australia's Taylah Robertson picked up a bronze in the women's flyweight category on the Gold Coast in 2018 despite losing her bout to England's Lisa Whiteside.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
