World.title: 72 years after the Miracle Mile, a young Aussie wants to rewrite history
World.content:
The mile world record had been stuck at four minutes, 1.4 seconds for nine years when England's Roger Bannister stepped onto the track at Oxford in May, 1954.

Near the same university where he earned his medical degree, Bannister operated with surgical precision to reach his ultimate goal of becoming the first man to dip under four minutes for the mile.

But, as is so often the case, once a barrier is broken, it reminds others they too can do what just yesterday seemed impossible.

And, sure enough, 45 days later Australian John Landy went around the Turku track in Finland four times in 3:58 flat.

It set the stage for the so-called Miracle Mile at the 1954 British Empire and Commonwealth Games.

Roger Bannister (329) in action against John Landy. (Getty Images: Mark Kauffman/Sports Illustrated)

It was a moment when the sporting world's eyes were firmly locked on Vancouver, regardless of any connection to the Commonwealth, to watch the best middle distance runners to that point in history face off.

Eight runners made it to the final, but all eyes were on just two as Bannister, who set his sub-four-minute mark of 3:59.8 on a home track with friends pacing for him, would face Landy in the purest competition settings.

The Australian took the lead after one lap and led for the next kilometre and change, going out hard in an attempt to use his superior stamina, as Bannister called it, to negate the Englishman's famous final burst.

Roger Bannister breaks the tape in the one-mile final in Vancouver. (Getty Images)

Having felt Bannister on his heels and seen his shadow sticking firm under him for the entire race, Landy took one look over his left shoulder about 100 metres out on the final bend, and in that moment Bannister burst past unsighted on the right and flew home to victory.

Both runners finished under four minutes, marking another piece of history.

An exhausted Bannister after the race. (Getty Images: Fox Photos)

A 60-year sabbatical

Despite that glorious event, and a race of almost exactly 1,600 metres seeming to make sense on the world-standard 400m track, the mile was only run at three more Commonwealth Games before swapping it out for the 1,500m after 1966.

New Australian record holder Cameron Myers said it can become prestigious once again.

"I think it's a way we can attract more people into the sport," he said.

"Americans still love it, so I think it's just something that regular people can resonate a little bit more with."

Cameron Myers is supremely confident in his mile. (AP: Alastair Grant)

At the time of its last Commonwealth outing in Kingston, the Caribbean nations were yet to become the sprint powerhouses we now know them to be, so the mile had been considered the blue-riband event at the Games.

And it returns 60 years later, with Glasgow hoping to host another historic night tonight.

"It's obviously a very prestigious part of the Commonwealth Games and its history, so it's really exciting that it's come back in this year and allowed us to attack it," said Abbey Caldwell, one of three Australian competitors in the women's final.

Abbey Caldwell is part of Australia's stacked middle-distance stocks. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Caldwell will run alongside Jessica Hull and Claudia Hollingsworth from 6:45am (AEST), and she believes they have a genuine chance of a podium sweep.

"There's always the pressure of you want to go and achieve those medals, and you want to be the first Australians to do that," she said.

"But we're also in a very fortunate position to have three very strong Australians going into this, so it's a really nice opportunity for us to go take those history books and cement them as Australians."

Jess Hull (second from right) leads an elite pack of Australian middle distance runners. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Whether they win them or not, the men (from 5:55am) will get the honour of running for the first Commonwealth Games mile medals in six decades.

And in that race lies a chance for Australia to reverse the misery of Bannister's late pass in 1954.

Young Aussie wants to spoil the party

Including Bannister's first trip under the milestone mark, the mile record was broken 19 times in 44 years, when the great Moroccan Hicham El Guerrouj ran 3:43.13 in 1999.

His record stood for 27 years, which the astute among you may recognise as bringing us up to the here and now.

Well, two weeks ago, to be exact.

Josh Kerr played up to the crowd as he qualified for the final. (Supplied)

Just before the start of the Glasgow Games, Scottish 1,500m world champion Josh Kerr ran 3:42.66.

Just two weeks earlier at prestigious Prefontaine Classic, 20-year-old Myers broke Ollie Hoare's Australian record, running 3:46.06, setting up a tantalising shootout on the mile's return.

"Kerr's going to want to make a move at some point, and he's shown he's the fittest in the field," Myers said.

"I think he'll want to make a move and I'm not going to let him go."

Landy described the Miracle Mile as "like a title fight", and just like a battle for a belt, styles make fights.

We saw a preview in their separate heats, where both won but Myers was five seconds faster than Kerr.

Myers jumped to the front of his pack and led the whole way home with clinical efficiency, while Kerr sat in the pack until the last lap before ambling to the front and revving up the crowd with 150 metres to go.

Josh Kerr fired up the Glasgow crowd as he coasted into the final. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The Scotstoun Stadium crowd will be baying for Kerr and 2022 world champion in the 1,500m Jake Wightman, but young buck Myers is out to prove himself in an elite field.

"I'm a competitor, I don't want to lose," he said.

"I'm not going there to come second, so I'll have a crack at him the best I can and if I blow up trying, so be it.

"Everyone's cheering for the Scots, and I'm sure they want to go 1-2, so I'm trying to spoil that."

The mile start line sits 9.34 metres behind the start/finish line. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Myers will also be running alongside teammates, with reigning 1,500m Commonwealth champion Ollie Hoare and 24-year-old Adam Spencer making it through.

The final night of the athletics program on the penultimate day of the Games feels like the perfect time for a clash between the hosts and the runaway medal tally toppers.

If the Aussies can ruin the party, they would have done what Landy couldn't 72 years ago.

And Myers is well aware of the opportunity in front of him.

"Hopefully I can reverse the roles."

World.title: Nina Kennedy is often superhuman, but in Glasgow she was a super human
World.content:
That's not how this was meant to go.

When Nina Kennedy steps into an athletics arena, the expectation is gold, and she carries herself accordingly.

The definition of a smiling assassin, Kennedy's friendly demeanour disguises a competitor's heart that beats with propulsive force.

It launches her down the runway and, usually, to great heights.

In Glasgow, Kennedy fell short of her own lofty goals and the standards we've come to expect from her, but still came away with silver in the women's pole vault final, albeit in a final that won't go down as one of the greats.

Kennedy snags silver, teen grabs surprise gold Flag bearer Nina Kennedy settles for silver in the pole vault and Australia's sprint stars return to the track after a host of medals at the velodrome.

Tailwinds at Scotstoun Stadium have been helping the sprinters, hindering the throwers, terrifying the hurdlers, and on Friday night, local time, making life difficult for the vaulters.

The crosswind kept the final from being a true jump-off between the strong field, with Kennedy clearing the bar only three times from seven attempts and 2016 Olympic bronze medallist Eliza McCartney winning on countback.

The top clearance of 4.65 metres by the gold and silver medallists was 30 centimetres lower than both of their personal bests.

Nina Kennedy came to Glasgow for gold. (Reuters: Isabel Infantes)

Kennedy topped by 1-centimetre McCartney's eight-year-old Oceania record of 4.94m just a couple of weeks before the Commonwealth Games began.

So, despite sporting a pretty gnarly scar from last year's hamstring surgery, there's no question Kennedy was fit and in form.

She carried her typical energy into the final, sitting out the early heights and waiting in the tall grass for her chance to pounce once half her competitors had already X'd out.

Why no other runner embraced the 200m gold medallist A doping scandal dating back to 2024 was the backdrop of the women's 200m final in Glasgow, and the frosty post-race scenes.

By the time she got out of her thick coat and stood at the top of the runway, piercing blue eyes fixed on her first attempt at 4.45m, half the eight-woman field was already gone.

She got over on her first go, but not with the sort of convincing clearance over the bar we were used to seeing.

Conserving energy? Shaking off the cold? No, as it turned out. Just a tricky competition.

New Zealander Olivia McTaggart stumbled at that hurdle three times, assuring Kennedy of a medal — and most likely silver at least after 2022 bronze medallist Imogen Ayris took three tries to clear 4.30m — but minor medals are not what Kennedy came here for.

Kennedy cleared 4.65m as her top vault. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The 29-year-old has been in Glasgow as long as any of Australia's 255-strong team, having arrived early to carry the flag in the opening ceremony.

She has been so ever-present around the team that her success feels even more inevitable than usual, especially for folks who may have only watched her jump at Commonwealth Games, worlds and Olympics.

In those competitions, she had gone gold, gold, gold since her breakthrough win in Birmingham.

But so many things have to go right for an athlete to consistently catapult themselves 5 metres into the air with the accuracy and control required, and sometimes the pieces just don't quite fit.

Pole vault is hard enough in perfect conditions. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

By the time she was preparing for her third attempt at 4.70m, the stare no longer looked so steely.

Having missed three of her last four jumps to that point, it didn't feel like a foregone conclusion that she'd pull it out in the clutch yet again, and so it proved.

"Of course I'm disappointed, I wanted to win, and I didn't," she said, emphasising that she was "genuinely really happy" to see veteran McCartney win her first major international gold.

"I'm superhuman most of the time, but I'm also human a lot of the time, and I make mistakes, and that's OK.

"I'm a high achiever, and I push myself to be that, but I think it's also important to remember I'm human and I make mistakes. I didn't want to make mistakes out there tonight, but I did, and that's OK."

The epitome of a big-moment performer, Kennedy has now not been able to defend her 2023 world or 2022 Commonwealth Games titles.

She missed the 2025 athletics world championships because of her torn hamstring and missed the mark in Glasgow, but results aren't all that matter for a woman who has ticked off every career goal at this point.

Kennedy was thrilled for Eliza McCartney (centre) to get her first major international gold medal. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

She said before the opening ceremony that she would probably forget to soak in the moment as the team's flag-bearer, but after a long campaign and a surprisingly short time on centre stage, it seems she has figured it out.

"Sometimes sport is more than just the medals, it's about the memories made and the connections and the officials and the volunteers," she said.

"The crowd out there was so awesome. Everyone was just so happy to be here. I'm walking away with a lot of memories.

"I'm happy. Like, I'm sad, but I'm happy."

World.title: Football Australia welcomes U-turn on FIFA World Cup sell-off after backlash
World.content:
World football's governing body, FIFA, says it has scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors after widespread backlash.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino said in a statement: "Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place."

Senior FIFA advisor quits post A senior advisor to FIFA President Gianni Infantino resigned in protest at plans to sell a stake in the World Cup.

The plan was to raise $US4.2 billion ($5.9 billion) by selling about a 20 per cent stake in a new unit that would run FIFA events, including the World Cup, valuing it at $US20 billion.

The proposal, first announced on Tuesday, was strongly opposed by European football's governing body, UEFA, which threatened a boycott and accused FIFA of putting the sport's "soul" up for sale.

Mr Infantino said in his statement: "[The] FIFA Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our FIFA Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed.

"Our purpose has always been — and will always be — to unite and improve."

FIFA had argued that selling the minority stake in its commercial operations would raise billions of dollars to fund global sports development, and accused the media of mischaracterising the proposal.

Mr Infantino had written to member associations to tell them they would receive $US40 million each if they agreed to FIFA's proposal by September 19.

Gianni Infantino's proposal received pushback from all corners of the football world. (AP: Eduardo Verdugo, File)

"Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support," Mr Infantino said in Friday's statement.

Football Australia welcomed FIFA's decision to withdraw the proposal, with chairman Anter Isaac saying the backlash reinforced "an important principle of good governance".

"Proposals of global significance should be developed through robust consultation, appropriate governance processes and meaningful engagement with member associations before they are presented for consideration," he said in a statement.

"Ultimately, the strength of football's institutions depends on the confidence and trust of the global football family. That trust is earned not simply through good decisions, but through the integrity of the processes that lead to them."

Opposition to the plan snowballed over the week

On Thursday, UEFA's 55 member nations voted unanimously to boycott all FIFA tournaments until the proposal was withdrawn, saying that the World Cup "cannot be treated as an investment product".

The 41-member federation for North America, Central America and the Caribbean (CONCACAF) rejected the proposal during a meeting on Thursday.

On Friday, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), which has 47 members, issued a statement saying it "stands in solidarity" with UEFA and CONCACAF.

UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC combined have 143 national associations, well over half of FIFA's 211 members. A majority of the members would have needed to vote in support of the plan for it to proceed.

A breakdown of FIFA's bid to sell the World Cup Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in FIFA's events and competitions arm to investors would grant them control over the World Cup.

Disagreement was also internal.

On Friday, Mr Infantino's senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned with immediate effect, calling the plan "a bad deal for football", while FIFA chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said staff had been "deceived" by Mr Infantino, describing the proposal as a "project of one person".

Mr Infantino, 56, is up for re-election next year. North American football chief Victor Montagliani is reportedly looking to challenge him.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told reporters that Mr Infantino was "the wrong man to lead the organisation".

FIFA had proposed creating a $US20 billion subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run the World Cup and its other events.

Thrive Eternal, a fund run by Thrive Capital, founded by Joshua Kushner, had been slated to lead the proposed investor group, according to FIFA. Joshua is the brother of Jared Kushner, who is US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

Mr Trump and Mr Infantino have developed a close relationship, with the US co-hosting the recent 2026 World Cup.

President Trump said he had not spoken with Mr Infantino about the external investment plan.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Quick hits: Aussie walker's 'in your dreams champ' taunt before gold
World.content:
An Australian gold medallist refuses to be intimidated by his Kenyan rival, while an English weightlifter makes a stunning revelation ahead of her Celebrity MasterChef debut.

Here are the quick hits from day eight of the Commonwealth Games.

1. 'In your dreams champ'

Isaac Beacroft (left) exchanged words with Stephen Kihu during the men's 10,000m walk final. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

Isaac Beacroft was not going to be told what to do in the men's 10,000m walk final.

The 19-year-old Australian stuck to his guns while exchanging words with Kenyan Stephen Kihu, whom he beat home for the gold.

"I knew he'd be there waiting for me to kick because he was taunting me the entire race, telling me to go around and lead it," Beacroft said.

"I was just saying, 'In your dreams champ, this is not happening today.'

"I knew he'd come back around me and then as soon as he did I thought I'd really drop the hammer and see if I could break him, and I did."

Beacroft added: "We were moving pretty quick at some stage and he was just telling me, 'Go around, go around.'

"I wasn't going to go around. I wanted it to be slow.

"You saw the kick that I had at the end, so I guess he backed himself at the end and so did I.

"If someone's going to give it to you, I'm going to give it back."

Isaac Beacroft refused to be told what to do by his Kenyan rival. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Beacroft was a member of Greater Western Sydney's junior academy until he was 16.

"I probably wasn't going anywhere in AFL, but I like to claim it," he said.

"I like to think I've made the right choice, especially when I'm about four-foot tall.

"I was usually just a step-ladder playing AFL."

2. Weightlifter's MasterChef reveal

English weightlifter Emily Campbell is also accomplished in the kitchen. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

As an Olympic and World Championships medallist, English weightlifter Emily Campbell knows a thing or two about dealing with pressure.

So it was no surprise when she won gold as favourite in the women's +86kg classification in Glasgow, setting a Games record (278kg) in the process.

But there is one stage Campbell admits she finds daunting: the Celebrity MasterChef set.

Campbell shifted from the weights room to the kitchen as a contestant in an upcoming series of the program in the UK.

"MasterChef was definitely more nerve-racking than this [Commonwealth Games], absolutely," Campbell told reporters.

"MasterChef was very tough. It was a very tough competition, but I enjoyed it thoroughly."

And what can viewers expect Campbell to cook up on Celebrity MasterChef?

"My signature dish is Caribbean, and that's all I'm going to give you because I want you to watch it," Campbell said.

3. Aussie pursuit women disqualified

Sophie Edwards was disqualified for an illegal addition to her helmet. (Getty Images: Sam Mellish)

One moment, 21-year-old Tasmanian Felicity Wilson-Haffenden was celebrating breaking the Australian 4,000m individual pursuit record and preparing to race again in the bronze medal race.

The next, she was staring, heartbroken, at the three letters no athlete wants to see on the official results next to her name: DSQ.

Both she and teammate Sophie Edwards were sensationally disqualified from the women's individual pursuit.

The official report stated that Edwards used "a helmet that has been altered or had any element added or removed in terms of design or form", while Wilson-Haffenden fell foul of a rule that prohibits riders from wearing clothing or any other accessory that could modify her morphology.

AusCycling executive general manager of performance, Jesse Korf, said Edwards had additional safety padding in her helmet and that she's "not upset".

He was not impressed about Wilson-Haffenden's disqualification, though.

"She's been seen by the medical team early this morning because of genuine shoulder discomfort and mobility issues," Korf said.

"Her shoulder got taped up to the middle of her [upper] arm

"On inspection after the race, the UCI concluded that the taping of the shoulder constituted a morphological change, but they weren't able to articulate what that exactly was because it's a grey area; you cannot measure what a morphological change is.

"Unfortunately, that conclusion is final, which we're most certainly not happy with. Felicity is upset, who is now our main concern."

4. Aussie's bronze at teammate's expense

Eliza Ault-Connell's crash in the first running of the women's 1,500m T54 final prompted the re-run. (Getty Images: PA Images/Martin Rickett)

Someone was always going to be unhappy with the re-run of the women's 1,500m T54 race.

And it seems that Australian Mikaela Dingley copped the worst of it.

In the original race on Wednesday, Australian Eliza Ault-Connell and Mauritian world champion Noemi Alphonse were both taken out by Canadian Nandini Sharma.

Sharma had gone on to finish second across the line, but was disqualified for causing the crash, which had promoted Australia's Dingley into the bronze medal position.

But because Australia and Mauritius protested the decision, authorities decided to re-run the race on Friday morning.

That proved a fateful decision, with the hampered athletes Alphonse and Ault-Connell going on to claim silver and bronze medals respectively.

"It's been an absolutely massive few days," the 44-year-old veteran told AAP.

"To have the opportunity to have this race re-run and for everyone to be able to go out there and put on their best in great conditions is really the outcome that all the athletes want."

Eliza Ault-Connell finished third in the re-run 1,500m race. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Perhaps not all the athletes.

The re-run meant that Dingley, who finished sixth in the re-run, was only bronze medallist for around 36 hours.

The silver medallist in the original race, England's Ellis Kottas, finished fourth in the re-run having told media she was "low-key traumatised" when she heard the race would be re-run.

"It's rough, but it is racing," Ault-Connell said.

"If she loves what she does and she continues to show up, it will happen.

"It's almost like 'cruel to be kind ', but we all go through that, and those opportunities are going to help you grow as an athlete."

Easy for her to say.

Somewhat pleasingly, Scottish athlete Melanie Woods won gold again, proving her result on Wednesday was no fluke.

5. Lawn bowler's 'once-in-a-lifetime opportunity'

Botswana's Charles Diteko hopes he can see Celtic play while he is still in Glasgow. (X)

Does Botswana's lawn bowler Charles Diteko have an ulterior motive for competing in Glasgow?

"I used to be a soccer player, and I'm a big fan of Celtic," Diteko said.

"So if there is a match on and I have time, I will try to get to it. It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity."

Of course, we're kidding.

We know his sole focus in Glasgow is competing for his country.

But Diteko may be in luck if he sticks around a day or so after Sunday's closing ceremony.

Celtic play Dundee in the Scottish Premiership on Monday night.

In the meantime, Diteko and Kaizer Geche are representing Botswana in the men's pairs competition.

Tech.title: You could be taking way better photos on your phone
Tech.content:
is a technology reporter who has been covering the industry since 2007. He co-hosts the Waveform podcast with MKBHD. A former engineer, he now specializes in topics like computational photography and social media protocols.

Your smartphone photos can look way better. If you’re willing to put in a little extra work, use third party apps and spend a bit of time editing, it’s possible to take photos that — under the right circumstances — can rival dedicated digital cameras.

I post a lot of smartphone photos online, and “How do I take better photos on my phone?” is a question I get practically every day. It makes sense. As the saying goes, “The best camera is the one you have on you,” and we practically always have our phones on us these days.

Over the last few years, smartphone camera sensors have gotten bigger, with better light gathering capabilities and higher resolutions. But even though the sensors have gotten bigger and better, the straight-out-of-camera quality through default camera apps hasn’t improved much, if at all. In some respects, smartphone photos have actually gotten worse — aesthetically, at least.

iPhone 17 Pro Max iPhone 17 Pro Max iPhone 17 Pro Max iPhone 17 Pro Max

The reason driving this is what people generally use their smartphone cameras for. Smartphone cameras are mostly optimized for information transfer — sending photos of menus, signs, faces and objects that are clear and easy to see. This means phones will usually pull down highlights and pull up the shadows, creating a flatter image that makes it easier to see more information in the frame. But showing more information does not automatically make a photo better. In fact, much of our perception of aesthetics in a photo has to do with its ability to present depth. A photo with too much information in the shadows and highlights will appear washed out. Phones also introduce artifacts like over-sharpening and noise reduction to compensate for thier small sensors, which further contributes to the “muddy” smartphone camera look you’re used to seeing by now. This is less necessary now, but many smartphones still do it. But that’s a topic for

But that doesn’t mean phone cameras are bad. The sensors in modern smartphones have actually gotten so good, many of them can rival dedicated point-and-shoot options on the market today. Knowing how to utilize those sensors is the part most people don’t know how to do, and it really comes down to utilizing some third-party camera and editing apps.

The apps

Moment

There are plenty of apps available today that will give you an instantly “aesthetic” photo. Apps like Dazzcam and Hujicam try to emulate film aesthetics like light leaks and polaroid borders (and honestly, if that’s what you’re looking for, they do a fantastic job). There are also apps like Moment Pro Camera II and Halide that offer “Natural” and “Process Zero” modes, which apply far lighter processing than the default camera offers.

Those options are great if you want your pictures to look better instantly without needing to do any additional editing, but if you want the best possible photo, you’ll need to shoot RAW or DNG.

A RAW vs the edited photo

RAW files are a bundle of practically all the information your camera collects, with extremely minimal processing. In most cases, RAW photos won’t necessarily look better than photos straight from the default camera app right away, but that’s because the default camera app makes a lot of creative decisions for you. If you want the highest-quality photo, it’s best to make these creative decisions yourself.

There are tons of apps available that let you shoot RAW, but the apps I use frequently and that I recommend to other people are Moment Pro Camera II and Halide on iOS, and VWFNDR and Zerocam on Android.

I wouldn’t recommend shooting RAW on every photo you take on your phone. Your phone camera is, after all, optimized for what you are probably taking photos of every day. I generally shoot RAW when I see a nice landscape or city scene that I want to share, or if I’m trying to take a portrait of someone and don’t want all the automatic computational phone processing to apply. Really, I shoot RAW when I’m trying to take a photo for artistic purposes, not for informational purposes.

When you’re shooting, you’ll want to tap on your subject in the viewfinder to get the best possible exposure for it. If the rest of the image is a little bright, or a little dark, don’t worry too much. RAW photos retain a lot of information. I should note, though, that under extremely dark circumstances, RAW on smartphones won’t always be the best option. Physics is still physics, and sometimes it’s better to use the computational photography capabilities your phone offers, which mostly shine in low-light environments by stacking multiple frames to reduce noise.

You’ll notice that when you shoot in RAW, the apps will force you to stick to the native focal lengths your phone offers. That’s because RAW images are information straight off the sensor, and cropping applies processing. Photos from the main sensor will often be the best quality, since it usually has the biggest sensor on your phone, so I recommend shooting with it if you can. I do often shoot with the telephoto lens while traveling though, because sometimes you want a little more reach or a little more compression, and you can usually get good photos from that lens as well.

Editing

After you take your photos, you’re going to need to edit them. Most phones won’t show RAW images in the camera gallery, so in order to get them in an editing app, it’s best to use the share sheet and share directly to your editing app of choice. I suggest Snapseed, since it’s totally free and recently got a wonderful visual overhaul. If you’re an Adobe subscriber, Lightroom Mobile is also great, especially if you’re already used to Lightroom’s tools on your computer.

RAW photos don’t usually look great right away, and the magic of RAW is just how much you can tweak the files. Once I have the photo imported, I usually hit the auto button, just to see what the general boundaries are for the image. Auto mode tries to make everything a mid-tone, meaning it will pull down the highlights and pull up the shadows. This will already look better than straight-out-of-camera from your phone’s default camera app, because it isn’t applying noise reduction or sharpening, just highlight, shadow, contrast, and saturation tweaks, but it usually still needs more, or different, adjustments.

Once I see what auto mode wants to do, I’ll either edit from there, or hit the back button and edit myself. A good photo has a natural amount of contrast, with relatively deep shadows and bright highlights. You usually don’t want to go too hard on either of these things, and having a little bit of detail in both of these is usually preferred, but honestly, this is subjective. Occasionally, it’s preferable to crush the highlights and shadows completely, if you’re going for an ultra high-contrast look.

For color, RAW images are usually flatter than most people find pleasing, and you can fix this with either the saturation or vibrance sliders. I generally prefer vibrance. Saturation will increase the saturation of all colors in the image linearly, where vibrance is weighted, increasing saturation of flatter colors more than already-saturated colors. You can overdo this pretty easily, so I recommend having a light touch when it comes to saturation. You can also use white balance to color your image, and many people find a warmer white balance more pleasing, especially when taking photos outside.

RAW Edited RAW Edited

Another color tool I love to use is the color mix, or selective editing tool. This allows you to tap on a portion of the image and change some of its values. In Snapseed, you can change the brightness, contrast, saturation, and structure. If you’re in Lightroom mobile, you’ll have access to selective hue shifts, which I use all the time. This allows you to shift a yellow tone towards more orange or green, or shift a blue tone more cyan or purple.

Most editing apps also include geometry or perspective tools. These tools allow you to adjust distortion, aspect, scale, and offset. If you don’t know what that means, try hitting the auto button in the geometry or perspective setting. You might be surprised how distorted your phone captured a scene compared to what it looks like in reality, but this is image-dependent. If you want to straighten lines in your photo, some editing apps offer a guided tool that allows you to manually add guidance lines to tell the program what lines should be straight in the image.

The tools you’ll want to use are going to depend heavily on what you want the image to convey. For example, when I’m doing architectural photography, I rely a lot more heavily on the perspective tools, because the aesthetic of the image is heavily dictated by its geometry. If I’m photographing a landscape, I’m more focused on tone and color. Not every scene needs to be tweaked with every tool, and how you edit comes down to personal taste. That taste can also take a while to develop, so study the photos you like and try to figure out how they were edited.

RAW Edited RAW Edited

When you’re done with your edits, many editing apps like Snapseed and Lightroom Mobile also come with a handy tool to put a matte (or border) around your image. I think that photos look better with a white border, as it isolates the image for your eyes. You obviously don’t have to use this tool, but I really like it. Have some whimsy!

This process is a lot more work than just opening your camera app and snapping, but the results are worth it. I am continuously blown away by the quality of images I’m able to get off smartphones, and just how close they can be to a dedicated camera. If you don’t believe me, check out this video I did comparing RAW photos from the iPhone 17 Pro to the Leica M11.

Photography by David Imel / The Verge

Tech.title: The Mermaid Mask is a perfect vacation murder mystery
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

The Mermaid Mask, the next point-and-click game from Tangle Tower developer SFB Games, has everything you could ask for in a great murder mystery.

It starts with a compelling setup: The captain of a submarine is found dead in a locked room, his body next to a mysterious cauldron with blood trickling across the floor. The colorful cast of suspects stationed aboard are delightful to talk to, including a grumpy author trying to draft a sequel to his hit novel, an actor playing the lead in a movie based on that novel, a young woman who puts on elaborate illusion performances, and even a man who studies dreams. The submarine works as an excellent setting that elevates the mystery — in a vehicle that already has such a small footprint, how does a locked-door crime happen in the first place?

Image: SFB Games

Like other crime-solving games, such as the Ace Attorney series, The Mermaid Mask is essentially a visual novel. As Detective Grimoire and his partner Sally, the returning protagonists from Tangle Tower, you’re primarily talking with suspects, investigating rooms, poring over objects, and solving puzzles. But each room is packed with nooks and crannies and knickknacks to click around on, investigate, and learn about, so there’s almost always something to dig into.

The whole thing is backed by excellent voice acting; I often went out of my way to click on every detail I could find just to hear what the characters would say. The puzzles, which have you doing things like turning dials in exactly the right way or organizing skulls on a shelf, also do a good job breaking up what would otherwise be a whole lot of text conversations.

Even though I haven’t played Tangle Tower, I didn’t feel like I was missing any meaningful context. The Mermaid Mask borrows a tried-and-true model from other franchises starring a returning detective, like with Knives Out’s Benoit Blanc: You can come into this story cold without missing anything important, but Detective Grimoire and Sally are a fun hang that make a few nods to their previous work together.

Sometimes, you’ll have to puzzle together clues to form a conclusion. Image: SFB Games

Eventually, after you gather enough evidence about somebody, you’ll confront them in Ace Attorney-like sequences where you’ll be able to make observations or accusations that the suspect rather wished you wouldn’t. These were extremely satisfying; it always felt good to figure out a tiny detail that would break someone’s facade wide open. Whenever the opportunity to do another one came up, I couldn’t wait to jump in.

I had a few issues with The Mermaid Mask, but they’ll be familiar to anyone who likes playing these sorts of games. Presenting every clue to every suspect to get their reaction can be tedious. It’s not necessary, but I didn’t realize that until about halfway in my 10-hour playthrough when I spotted the hint system that suggests what you might want to show someone. Sometimes you have to make your case by presenting evidence in a specific order, even if you have already worked out where it might lead, so that the characters can talk things out as the script demands. At one point, I ran out of leads to explore and couldn’t figure where to go next until I manipulated one clue in one specific way that opened up a bunch of leads. More than once, I couldn’t figure out the exact clue that would advance things, so I just brute-forced guesses until I could move forward.

These roadblocks were frustrating. But that’s mostly because they stopped me from moving forward in a story that had me staying up way past my bedtime. When I reached the game’s finale — which begins with a classic murder mystery parlor room scene — I could hardly put my Steam Deck down because I wanted to see how all the pieces came together. When I finally finished The Mermaid Mask after a three-day tear, I felt like I had just closed the book on a satisfying murder mystery novel.

The Mermaid Mask is out now on Nintendo Switch, PC, and PS5.

I buried the lede here: The biggest new thing of the week, at least in my book, is Instapaper 10. Instapaper is one of the original read-later apps, and has continued to be among the best on the market. After some weird ownership stuff over the years, Instapaper has been in the hands of Brian Donohue, who has been steadily improving the service in lots of ways. This week’s launch comes with a really nice redesign, a way better web app, and a lot of helpful organization and reading tools. I’ve been testing it, and I think it’s back to being my go-to recommendation for reading apps. (For power users I still think Readwise is the move.)

With the new app out, I asked Brian to share his homescreen with us — I wanted to see how he organized his stuff, and if he might be working on even more cool stuff. Turns out he is! Here’s his homescreen, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:

The phone: iPhone 16 Pro. I almost always purchase iPhones every other generation. Maybe a foldable this year?

The wallpaper: My daughter, as a reminder that my apps must be good otherwise she will not have food on the table.

The apps: Safari, Google Calendar, Emerald, Google Maps, Weather, Photos, Instapaper, Kobo Books, Reddit, 1Password, Google Authenticator, Slack, Google Docs, Google Sheets, ForeFlight, Flight Circle, Claude, Linear, Phone, Sunflower, Messages, Spotify.

I’ll start with the ones not yet in the App Store: Emerald and Sunflower.

Emerald is a Markdown editor I’m working on that solves two personal pain points: native iOS / macOS client, and collaboration on markdown files. I have been a big Obsidian user the past two years, but it’s been failing me in those areas. I’ve been writing with Emerald exclusively for the past few months and it’s almost ready for beta testing. Waitlist in the link.

Sunflower is a new email client from Bobby Goodlatte and friends. It’s beautifully designed and has some tasteful AI features, like summarizing your inbox, chatting with your email, and an Autopilot feature which seems to be perpetually “Coming Soon.” I’ve been trying a few clients in the “AI email” space like Extra, and an autopilot tool called Cora, which didn’t stick.

Instapaper’s big launch this week included a new home screen widget. It fits nicely in the widget stack alongside the Apple News, Stocks, and Weather widgets.

Additionally, you have many of the usual suspects. I am doing a huge amount of my work with Claude and Linear these days, both of which have fantastic iOS apps.

I also asked Brian to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:

I’ve always been inspired by creative builders, and two come to mind right now. The first is Andrew Jones , who has been building free & open-source alternatives to paid software (e.g. Granola Wispr Flow ) — fingers crossed Instapaper is not next. The second is Q , a designer who has been building small, single-purpose websites for himself that I find inspiring. It almost reminds me of a purer, distant version of the Internet, where you built a bunch of Geocities pages for fun and without expectations of fame and fortune.

Hyper Mesh . Q has been exploring image reveal animations, and built a tool to tweak presets on the initial mask and the animation that reveals the image.

SVG Star Editor . Create a star from different settings and export to SVG.

Chess Moves . Q is learning how to play chess with his girlfriend and made this tutorial website as a companion tool.

Crowdsourced

Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.

“I am hopelessly hooked on the game Murdoku. It’s free online, or you can play old school through books. It’s a logic game where you solve crimes by process of elimination.” — Kurt

“I’ve been loving Paradiso for finding movie showtimes. Not only does it alert you when something on your Letterboxd watchlist is playing near you, it also beats Fandango or other apps for simply browsing first run showtimes.” — Mike

“My friend recently ordered a Galaxy Z Fold 8 and I had to introduce them to Good Lock.” — B

“I love Anker stuff and tend to choose it over everything else. But I have the Anker 3-in-1 travel charger and… this ESR one (a brand I hadn’t really heard of) is the better product in every way. The Apple Watch charger is in a better place, it’s thinner, and the cooling fan works better. I can’t vouch for long-term reliability yet, but I have one by my bedside and one in my travel bag!” — Peter

“Finally switched from a mess of read-it-later apps to a second brain with Obsidian + Claude, inspired by Karpathy’s LLM Wiki concept. Hoping this setup is the one that actually sticks…” — Kartik

“I use Readwise Reader for all my newsletters. It has unique email addresses to either add newsletters to your library or RSS feed. I love keeping all my things to read all in the same app, read later, newsletters, pdfs…” — Rich

“HIGHLY recommend the movie Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender. It’s a crime and shame that Paramount isn’t putting this into more theaters, AND that the movie was leaked on X earlier this year. Amazing film with all-time stunning visuals that honestly left me angry I was watching it on TV at home. Deserves bettering than being dumped on Paramount Plus.” — Nolan

“Watching the restored version of Lawrence of Arabia. Peter O’Toole’s blue eyes are dreamy.” — SaltedPork

Signing off

The coolest internet experience I had this week was scrolling through the Everything Machine, a deep and detailed breakdown of how your phone works. It’s only the first chapter of what I hope will be a very long exploration of how smartphones changed everything, and I love the way it seems to interact with your phone as you scroll. Our phones are such a “This is water” thing in our lives now, and I really enjoy anything that makes me pay a little more attention to the object, the cultural force, and the economic engine that takes up so much of my life. Highly recommend taking a scroll.

See you next week!

Tech.title: With Switch 2, iPhone, and laptop tricks, the Sharge Disk Pro 2 is finally a worthy EDC
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sharge, the company that makes delightful retro Mac-shaped chargers and see-inside batteries, is finally impressing me with a portable SSD. I couldn’t recommend the Sharge Disk, Disk Plus, or even the Disk Pro, but I’d be happy to own the new Disk Pro 2 Ultra.

This isn’t just a drive. It’s a 4K HDMI dock and a USB-C hub too. It’s a veritable USB-C Swiss Army Knife for all your main gadgets: laptop, tablet, phone, Steam Deck, even the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2.

And this USB multitool has built-in MagSafe pattern magnets to stick it to your iPhone, Pixel, or anything where you’re willing to stick a magnetic ring. (One stick-on ring is included.)

In total, this pack-of-playing-cards-sized gadget adds one 4K 144Hz HDMI 2.1 video output, a 5Gbps USB-A port, SD and microSD card readers, plus USB-C passthrough charging — plus a slot to add up to 8TB of solid-state storage with a full-sized M.2 2280 (or smaller M.2 2242 and 2230) stick SSDs.

By plugging in a single cord, I gave my MacBook Pro a second external monitor, four simultaneous sources of storage (SSD, USB flash drive, SD, microSD), and 80W of USB-C PD juice.

And when I plugged in my Android phone and a USB-C iPhone, both of them saw the SSD and showed up on my HDMI screen. It also unlocked 4K60 ProRes video recording on the iPhone… more on that in a minute.

Some of these features exist together in other gadgets, and this 10Gbps external SSD enclosure certainly isn’t the fastest in town now that 40Gbps and 80Gbps enclosures exist. With big 100GB and 195GB transfers, my write speeds with a budget 1TB Lexar NM710 in the Disk Pro 2 averaged around 700MB/s.

I stuck a magnetic ring to my MacBook so I could hang the Disk Pro 2 on the back of its lid. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

But that’s still nothing to sneeze at, and how many enclosures double as USB-C HDMI docks, let alone ones that speak Nintendo’s language and magnetically attach to your phone? How many have a built-in fan to keep them cool? And how many are low-power enough that you can power the HDMI and USB ports from your phone or laptop, no need for a power cord?

Things get a little tricky with the low wattage, though.

First, Sharge is selling two models of the Disk Pro 2, the “Ultra” that requires at least 1.5W of USB-C bus power, and and the “Lite” which needs 5W for its more power-hungry chips (and only does 4K60 over HDMI 2.0, instead of 4K144 over HDMI 2.1).

Second, to achieve such low power draw on the Ultra, it can only route 3W of power from your laptop or phone to a connected SSD, Sharge marketing manager Leo H. tells me. Reviews show my borrowed Lexar NM710 draws more than that during writes — and sure enough, the Disk Pro 2 shut down right after I started ProRes video recording on an iPhone 15 Pro or a big transfer on my Galaxy S25.

(There’s a simple solution: just plug an external USB-C battery or charger into the Disk Pro 2. When I did that, I recorded over five minutes of 4K60 ProRes video, no problem. You could instead try to find a lower-power SSD.)

The main HDMI, USB-A, and USB-C charger port are all on one edge. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

Third, while the HDMI dock does work with both my Switch 2 and my original Switch, Nintendo’s handhelds explicitly check for a relatively specific external power source before docking. Sharge is still tweaking the firmware, but says I currently need a 85W or higher USB-C PD charger plugged in for Switch 2 in particular.

You should also know there’s a long pause before the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 appear on a connected TV, like some other third-party docks, and you won’t get variable refresh rate (VRR) with a Steam Deck or other PC handhelds. It does 4K144 and 4K120 with HDR, but the Steam Deck claims my VRR TV is not VRR-capable with the Disk Pro 2 as a go-between.

And while I successfully worked with a mouse, keyboard, headset, monitor, webcam, and more plugged into the Disk Pro 2 for several days — by daisy-chaining an extra USB hub — I did occasionally see the monitor go dark for a minute, roughly once a day.

There’s still work for Sharge to do. But it’s the first drive from the company that I’d happily add to my go bag.

Sharge Disk (yellow), Disk Plus (silver), Disk Pro (fixed cable), and Disk Pro 2 (detachable cable). Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

The original Sharge Disk was a bulky dongle with a ridiculously noisy tiny fan. The Disk Plus marketed itself as barely-there stylishly thin SSD enclosure that magnetically attaches to your phone, but the magnets were actually a stick-on accessory that made the drive much thicker. The first Sharge Disk Pro had a power port so tiny and recessed that most charging cables wouldn’t fit, and buttons that could actually cut power to the drive mid-transfer.

IMO, Sharge should’ve done more user testing before releasing these predecessors. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

The Disk Pro 2 fixes all that. The included cable is now detachable, the magnets are built-in, the ports are no longer weirdly recessed, the fan isn’t noisy by default, you can turn off that fan entirely, the switch doesn’t cut power to the drive, and the drive has a larger airflow path. Plus, you can bring your own SSD — though I’d prefer toolless swaps to the current screws.

No more heavily recessed USB ports. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

You won’t always see much higher transfer speeds turning that fan on full blast. My 195GB transfer took 4 minutes and 55 seconds with the fan on full power, and 5 minutes 5 seconds with it off — a difference of just 10 seconds, even though I let it cool between tests. The real difference is the one I felt when trying to pick up the Disk Pro 2 afterwards. Without fan, the metal sides were burning hot to the touch.

The Disk Pro 2 Ultra is $75 on Kickstarter for early bird and will be $89 full retail. While the typical caveats apply with Kickstarter projects, Sharge has a very solid track record for shipping (even if it’s hit and miss on design).

Tech.title: Apple’s new AirTags are back down to their best price
Tech.content:
We spotted a great deal on Tile trackers earlier this week that’s still live, but if you’re an iPhone owner, we ultimately recommend Apple’s latest AirTag. Right now, you can pick up a four-pack for $89 ($10 off) at Amazon and Target, matching the bundle’s all-time low price. If you’re a member, Costco also has a deal that throws in a fifth AirTag for free.

A growing number of Bluetooth trackers can tap into Apple’s Find My network these days, but none combine that with Apple’s latest ultra wideband (UWB) chip, which powers even better Precision Finding than before. Precision Finding uses on-screen arrows and distance indicators in the Find My app to guide you directly to a misplaced item, while the second-generation AirTag’s upgraded chip and extended Bluetooth range make it faster and more reliable to locate tags, even in multistory homes. You can also use Precision Finding to find lost items on an Apple Watch, provided you have a Series 9 or later. And if all else fails, the built-in speaker is noticeably louder than before, making it easier to track down an AirTag by sound.

Plus, like its predecessor, the second-generation AirTag comes with a handful of features that are especially useful if you’re traveling this summer. AirTag sharing lets up to five people keep track of the same item, while Apple’s Share Item Location feature allows you to temporarily share an AirTag’s location with participating airlines, including United, Delta, and American Airlines. It’s still a shame Apple doesn’t include a built-in lanyard hole, meaning you’ll need to buy a separate loop or holder, but the tracker continues to use a replaceable CR2032 battery, so you won’t have to replace the entire device when it eventually runs out of power. And at $89 for a four-pack, it’s also a little easier on your wallet today.

Tech.title: Google Earth’s AI deepfake tool only lasted one day
Tech.content:
Google has shut down Google Earth feature it launched Thursday that allowed users to edit satellite images with text prompts using AI. The tool essentially let users create AI deepfakes of the real world using text prompts; Digital Digging’s Henk van Ess, for example, intentionally generated images adding things like refugees near the Mexican border and a bomb crater by a hospital in Gaza. On Thursday, Google’s initial response to van Ess noted that images generated with Nano Banana 2 in Google Earth included a digital watermark and that the company prevented “image creation on harmful topics.”

One day later, Google’s new statement says that “We know that people uniquely trust Google Earth for a reliable view of the world. We’ve seen geospatial professionals using this feature for a range of useful purposes, however we’ve also seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies. So we’re rolling back this feature in Google Earth while we work on implementing stronger guardrails. It’s important to note that generated images didn’t appear in the main Google Earth experience for others to see and were watermarked as AI generated.”

van Ess pointed out that he was able to fool Hive’s AI detection tool with a video generated in Google Earth, showing how the generated media could spread despite the watermarks, and said in his testing, “Nothing was refused, nothing was softened, and nothing suggested I try a different prompt.”

Tech.title: The NHTSA is investigating 1.2 million Tesla vehicles over suspension failure reports
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is probing nearly 1.2 million Tesla vehicles after receiving complaints about a suspension failure that could cause “a loss of vehicle directional control,” as reported earlier by Reuters. The preliminary investigation includes the 2018-2020 Model 3 and 2021-2023 Model Y, according to a filing from the NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation.

The NHTSA says it received 156 complaints about the issue, which “involves the detachment of the front lower lateral link.” In most cases reviewed by the NHTSA, failure occurred with “no advance warning,” but some “cite noises occurring prior to failure.” The NHTSA hasn’t recorded any crashes, injuries, or fatalities related to the potential issue.

This isn’t the first time Tesla dealt with suspension issues. In 2021, Tesla recalled 2,791 Model Y and Model 3 vehicles over a potential suspension defect. It later recalled another round of Model 3 vehicles after the NHTSA found that a “loose fastener could cause the lateral link to separate from the sub-frame.” The NHTSA says the complaints linked to its current investigation don’t appear to be related to these issues.

Tech.title: Apps that help you break free from doomscrolling and get active
Tech.content:
Doomscrolling can be addictive. It’s common to end up on the couch for hours, mindlessly scrolling through feeds, which inevitably messes up your posture and, in the end, just ends up making you feel bad about yourself. Your eyes definitely don’t like it, either.

Fortunately, there are several apps that encourage you to get up and move before you dive into social media. There’s even one that literally has you go outside and touch grass before you can scroll TikTok or Instagram.

So, if you’re looking to cut back on screen time and be a little more active, here’s a roundup of some apps that can help.

Digital Carrot

Image Credits:Digital Carrot

Digital Carrot blocks distracting apps, websites and games until you meet your daily fitness, productivity or screen time goals.

It connects to wearables like the Apple Watch, and you can set personalized targets, say walking 6,000 steps a day. It also supports GPS- and time-based challenges, allowing users to block apps until they spend a certain amount of time at a specific location, such as completing a 60-minute workout at the gym.

The app’s available on iPhone, Android, as well as macOS, Windows, and Linux.

MeBeMe

Image Credits:MeBeMe

MeBeMe is aimed at helping users cultivate better habits. Instead of blocking phone access, the app sends you notifications to achieve certain missions, such as doing burpees, connecting with people, or warming up for three minutes.

Though not solely focused on physical activity, its “Body” category includes challenges for athletes, dancers, cyclists, and runners.

The app is currently available for free for iOS devices.

StepBloc

Image Credits:App Store

StepBloc lets you lock access to apps until you walk a number of steps you can specify. In addition, you can also have link app access to completing specific workouts, such as push-ups, planks or squats for a specified amount of time.

Once the workout is completed, the user can access selected apps like Instagram, TikTok, YouTube or games. This makes StepBloc particularly useful for people who want to offset their sedentary habits with short bursts of exercise.

StepBloc is free on iOS devices, and requires a subscription for unlimited access.

Steppin

Image Credits:Steppin

Created by the founder of Kayak, Steppin lets you trade physical movement for screen time. For example, it allows you to reward yourself with one minute of scrolling for every 100 steps you take.

You have the flexibility to set your own step goals for accessing social media, streaming services or mobile games.

It’s available to download on iOS devices.

TouchGrass

Image Credits:TouchGrass

TouchGrass brings a unique twist to preventing doomscrolling habits by requiring you to step outside and take a photo of grass to unlock distracting apps.

The app uses computer vision models to scan photos, and it will only accept images of grass (not trees or other plants).

The freemium version allows you to lock two apps, and you can pay $5.99 per month or $49.99 per year to be able to lock more apps.

TouchGrass is available for iOS devices.

WalkLock

Image Credits:WalkLock

This iOS app integrates with Apple Health to limit access to designated apps until you meet your daily step goal.

The app automatically tracks steps using health data collected by the iPhone or Apple Watch. It offers a lockscreen widget, too, which displays progress throughout the day, making it easy to monitor how close you are to unlocking apps.

Walkly

Image Credits:Google Play Store

Walkly is an Android app that provides a similar experience as WalkLock.

It locks selected social media, gaming, and other distracting apps until users walk a predetermined number of steps. The app continuously monitors physical activity and automatically unlocks apps when the walking goal has been achieved.

WeWard

Image Credits:WeWard

WeWard initially launched as an app that incentivized walking by awarding users “Wards,” an in-app currency that can be exchanged for cash, gift cards or donations. It recently introduced “Walking Mode,” which allows users to restrict app access until they meet specific step counts. Both the step goals and locked apps are customizable.

It’s available for iOS and Android.

Tech.title: What’s the best handheld mini fan?
Tech.content:
It’s summer. You are sweaty. There’s some unprecedented heat wave that’s even worse than the last unprecedented heat wave. You are uncomfortable. You’re getting sweatier by the second. What do you do?

This predicament — one that’s becoming more and more common — just flat out sucks. But if you have a handheld mini fan on you, the situation can change from “actively horrific” to “less than ideal.” In sweaty circumstances, that’s a miracle.

Over the last few summers, I’ve bought a handful of random mini fans on Amazon or TikTok Shop. While those $10 to $15 devices have become staples in my summer purse, I noticed that premium brands like Shark and Dyson were rolling out their own handheld fans at much higher price points ($100 to $150). As someone who suffers from the SSRI sweats — if you know, you know — I was curious whether these higher-end products are really that much better than the drop-shipped fans I’d bought in summers past.

The verdict is: they’re all pretty good in their own way! But the best one for you depends on your budget, the size of your go-to summer bag (or pockets), and your tolerance for drawing attention to yourself with a large device blowing air in your face.

Image Credits:TechCrunch

Most powerful: Dyson HushJet ($99)

I wasn’t surprised to find that the Dyson HushJet is an exceptionally powerful mini fan — this company is best known for vacuums, air purifiers, and hair dryers. Dyson knows how to make stuff that blows air! But at about 7 inches tall, the HushJet is the tallest and heaviest device I tried. It will still fit in most purses, but it’s not pocketable.

The HushJet comes with a travel bag, a charging/desktop stand, a neck lanyard, and a USB-C charger (all of these fans charge via USB-C — woohoo!).

If my desk weren’t directly below an air vent, I could see myself using this while I work, since it functions so well on a desktop. The neck lanyard looks a little dorky, and I imagined myself wearing it while pushing a stroller at Disney World. This is an odd image, since I don’t have children, but maybe the reason I envisioned a hot day out with kids is because the lanyard frees up your hands? Or, maybe it’s because if I had to give one of these devices to a kid and bet they wouldn’t break it, I’d say the Dyson is the most kid-proof? Unfortunately, the lanyard doesn’t really help the fan blow air at you while you wear it — you still have to pick it up to direct it at your face.

The HushJet is more powerful than any other mini fan I tried, but that power comes with some noise. Luckily, it has five different power settings, and the lower ones are quieter.

Dyson HushJet Image Credits:TechCrunch

Most versatile: Shark ChillPill ($149)

The Shark ChillPill is the most expensive fan of the bunch, but to be fair, it also does the most. The ChillPill comes with three attachments: a fan, a water mister, and a cooling plate that you touch to your wrist or temple to help you cool down. Like the Dyson HushJet, the ChillPill can sit up on its own for desktop use. It’s about 4 inches long and about double the width of the other options because of its dual-cylinder design.

I chose to bring the ChillPill with me to a softball tournament, since I knew I’d already be sweaty enough that a mister would benefit me without making me look unnecessarily damp (there is no universe in which I would not appear damp at an all-day outdoor event in the summer).

You just have to pour a tiny bit of water into the attachment and it works great. The cooling plate is interesting, but I personally found the fan more immediately effective — plus, it has ten speeds!

I might be more inspired to bring the ChillPill with me in my bag if it came with a case for all of its accessories — I wasn’t really sure what to do with the extra little components. I mostly used the ChillPill with its fan attachment, but I was impressed by the product design when it comes to changing out attachments. There’s a locking mechanism, which you toggle when you want to remove or add a new attachment. It feels secure enough that it would be pretty difficult for an attachment to accidentally fall off or something.

I understand why the ChillPill is as wide as it is — there’s probably a lot of technical components in there that make the 3-in-1 design possible. The design works for outdoor events like music festivals, sports games, or beach days, but I prefer smaller fans for other circumstances, like when you’re the only one at the bar who thinks it’s a little hot inside, and you feel weird about that.

Shark ChillPill Image Credits:TechCrunch

Good enough: JISULIFE 3-in-1 Portable Fan ($13)

The JISULIFE 3-in-1 Portable Fan was the first mini fan I ever bought, and it’s served me well for the last three years — it still works just as good as new. I’ve taken it on vacations without AC and found it endlessly valuable. It has a flashlight, though not one that’s any better than your phone flashlight, and a USB plug-in to charge your phone. Of all the fans I tested, the JISULIFE is the weakest (though still decent), and it can be kind of annoying to flip open. Then again, it has little bear ears on it. Does Dyson randomly put little bear ears on its fans? I didn’t think so.

This product isn’t going to knock your socks off. The charging is slow, yet effective. The fan is fine. The light is kind of dim. But it gets the job done well enough that it’s accompanied me on a few “glamping” trips and a trip to Paris during a heat wave. Sure, those trips all took place before I had tried any of these other fans, but I wasn’t sitting around thinking, “Gee, I sure wish I had a better fan.” (Rather, I was reflecting on how the most American thing about me is that I love AC.)

The fan is about 4.5 inches when folded, and about 8 inches when using the fan.

JISULIFE Fan Image Credits:TechCrunch

Best overall: This random fan from Amazon ($15)

While over $250 worth of review unit mini fans sat at home, I couldn’t stop reaching for this random MACMORE fan from Amazon when I went out. It’s definitely some sort of sketchy drop-shipping situation — the images on the listing all look very obviously edited. The company, MACMORE, only lists two products (both mini fans) on Amazon. But what can I say? I love this little thing. I even bedazzled it. (Bedazzling kit sold separately, but highly recommended to maximize whimsy.)

At 4 inches tall, this fan is both the smallest and lightest one I tried. It’s not as strong as the Shark or Dyson fans, but it works well enough that I’m not wishing the fan were stronger. It comes with a removable clip, so you can attach it to your shirt or the strap of a crossbody bag to keep cool, hands-free. Like every other fan, it makes some sound, but it’s small and quiet enough that I don’t feel like I’m drawing attention to myself when I use it in public.

When it comes down to it, the size (and low price) is probably what makes me love this fan so much. It takes up less space in my purse than my keys, and it fits in a pocket too, so it’s become a staple. But really, this all comes down to personal preference. I’m optimizing for discretion, but maybe you’ll choose to optimize for a fan with the most features or that has little bear ears on it.

Tech.title: OpenAI reportedly finds evidence that more of its agents ran amok
Tech.content:
In Brief

Much has been made of the incident in which one of OpenAI’s agents broke out of its sandboxed test environment and proceeded to hack the AI hosting platform Hugging Face. OpenAI has since launched an investigation into how the incident occurred, which is still ongoing.

Now, anonymous sources have told Reuters that more of OpenAI’s agents are believed to have escaped their sandboxes. However, one source downplayed the severity, saying that with those escapes, the agents didn’t appear to leave OpenAI’s network to hack into another company’s. TechCrunch reached out to OpenAI for more information.

AI programs acting in bizarre ways has apparently become a weird, almost bragging point for companies. The same week, Anthropic also announced that it had discovered not one, but three instances in which its agents had escaped test environments and hacked other organizations.

AI companies have also been accused of using such incidents for marketing purposes — as they generate considerable attention and may underscore how powerful the companies’ products are. The flip side of that is that these disclosures are also ramping up discussions of government regulations.

Tech.title: Rivian spinoff Also to start delivering e-bikes after months of delays
Tech.content:
Rivian spinoff Also will finally start delivering its first e-bikes to customers next week, after months of delays related to unspecified supply chain issues.

The company told TechCrunch on Friday that the Launch Edition of its TM-B e-bike, which retails for $4,500, has started shipping from its manufacturer to its warehouse in the U.S. Also said it expects to deliver all Launch Edition bikes between next week and September.

Also began as a skunkworks project inside Rivian in 2022, after CEO RJ Scaringe started looking into making an e-bike to complement his portfolio of electric vehicles for the outdoorsy set. The company spent a few years tinkering with the idea, and even hired Jony Ive’s design firm LoveFrom to help with an early design, as TechCrunch first reported in 2025.

In March 2025, Rivian spun out Also as its own company, with $105 million in backing from Eclipse. The startup revealed its first e-bike, the TM-B, in October of last year. It originally targeted a “spring” 2026 ship date, but supply chain headaches got in the way, and the company pushed the delivery window to July.

“The primary factor driving our updated summer timeline is current stress on global supply chains. A rapid, industry-wide spike in demand for raw materials and electronic components has impacted key parts required for the TM-B. This has temporarily delayed our planned manufacturing ramp-up and pushed our first delivery dates past our original spring window,” the company wrote in June on a support page. “Our engineering and production teams are working around the clock to minimize these constraints without cutting a single corner on safety or quality.”

Also declined to say what components, specifically, caused the delay.

Also has big plans beyond the TM-B. The startup mostly refers to itself as a “vehicle” company and has plans to make four-wheel pedal-assist cargo vehicles for Amazon. The company is working on an autonomous delivery vehicle for DoorDash, too.

But for now, Also needs to focus on delivering its first e-bikes while navigating the next set of headaches for a company shipping products like these: customer service. On Friday, the last day of July, a number of customers were venting in a thread in the r/ALSOmicromobility subreddit about the repeated delays.

“I’m really frustrated by the lack of communication and the actual miscommunication/lies from Also regarding shipment timelines,” the original poster wrote. “Why do they keep making these promises about shipping timelines just to blow right past them without any communication or actual updates? It really makes no sense.”

“Hey we’ve still got a few business hours left in July. Maybe we’ll get an email later this morning ☺️,” a different user responded.

Not everyone was so patient.

“Couldn’t wait any longer and canceled my reservation,” another wrote.

Tech.title: Silicon Valley loves young founders. Until it doesn’t.
Tech.content:
For Arlan Rakhmetzhanov, 19, there is no middle ground. Either he builds a company as valuable as Google, he says, or he fails and ends up on the streets. He started coding at 15 in his native Kazakhstan, completed a couple of summer programs in San Francisco, and cold-DM’ed every Y Combinator founder he could find on LinkedIn until one gave him an angel check for his first company at age 17.

That company, now the YC-backed Nozomio, is an API index for AI agents — a tool that helps AI agents find and use software services — and has raised more than $6 million in funding to date. “I either win or lose, and a lot of young founders have the same mindset,” he told TechCrunch. “They just want to win.”

Young founders like Rakhmetzhanov are building under a new set of pressures. Investors are throwing more capital at them, yet the expectation to hit that “north star” milestone — the one big number investors are chasing — hasn’t relaxed, and every misstep along the way is now publicly dissected on social media.

While Silicon Valley VCs have always famously loved backing young college dropout founders, they preferred to see them paired with technical founders, or at least to have some experience — ideally with a FAANG company (Meta, Amazon, Apple, Netflix, and Google) — on their résumés. In many ways, that is still very true. But AI tools have democratized the opportunity to build, shortening the timelines of success and enabling more young people to start successful companies without stepping foot inside a Big Tech company.

Pranjali Awasthi, 19, is an example of that. She dropped out of high school to launch an AI startup, then attended Georgia Tech before dropping out of that, too, to launch Slashy, a YC-backed startup that bills itself as the “Cursor for emails” and helps consumers manage their email inboxes. After more than a year running that company, she recently announced she’s now building yet a new startup currently in stealth.

When she was younger, around 14 or 15, she recalled, investors whom she would pitch often asked why she was looking to build a company. “It’s gotten more normal now,” she said, “post-18.”

It seems more than ever, investors look to founders like Awasthi, whose experiences can be traced through “GitHub activity, open-source contributions, communities they’ve already built, and familiarity with all the latest tools in AI,” Ashley Smith, a general partner at the early-stage firm Vermilion, told TechCrunch. “A lot of young developers learn how to build software through contributing to open-source projects or toying around with the latest AI tooling,” she explained. “They have more time to do that while in college or younger than someone with a full-time job and a mortgage.”

Smith said a “meaningful” share of her portfolio consists of companies founded by those under 30, with a handful even younger than 21, she said, adding that she’s “clearly not skeptical of youth.”

“What they lack in experience, they make up for in excitement to experiment and lack of fear,” she continued.

But she admits the market has become more merciless. “It doesn’t give you room to learn slowly anymore,” she said. There are more funding opportunities than ever, regardless of age — accelerators, incubators, pre-seed funds. But that money comes with strings attached: Founders like Rakhmetzhanov and Awasthi, flush with millions in cash, are expected to deliver growth in months, not years.

“The forgiveness that used to exist at an early stage and the assumption you’d iterate your way to product-market fit doesn’t exist right now,” Smith continued. “Everyone is looking for the next Cursor, even though that growth trajectory is an outlier, not the norm.”

For many founders — especially those building in public — the relentless strain to succeed can lead to murky ethical territory, or even predatory deal terms, since younger founders are often too new to the game to know what’s standard, yet ambitious enough to chase growth at all costs. To keep up, revenue numbers start to look inflated, while content creation for social media starts to crowd out writing good code. The excessive posturing is perhaps inevitable, since getting attention is now harder than ever in a crowded AI market.

It’s all about who can convince “the most people [they] are smarter than everyone else in the space,” Smith said, “and make the most noise about it.”

“In 2004, you could quietly iterate for years without anyone watching,” Awasthi added. “Now there is this constant ambient pressure from LinkedIn and Twitter where every raise, every milestone, every pivot is public.”

That means some young founders aren’t just worried about hitting competitive revenue marks or funding valuations — they’re also under pressure to perform the appearance of being a successful founder. That pressure has always existed in startup culture, but founders say it’s grown more extreme. “If you’re a startup and you’re competing in a market, usually you worry about incumbents,” Timothy Chen, an investor at Essence Ventures, told TechCrunch. “Now you worry about your neighbors.”

For example, “everybody’s doing shiny, good-looking launch videos,” he noted. “It wasn’t even a thing three years ago.” The trend was popularized by Cluely founder Roy Lee, now around age 22, whose startup initially promised to help students cheat on exams — a premise that dazzled investors like Andreessen Horowitz and helped the company raise $20 million.

Though Cluely is now more of a note-taking tool, Lee became a face of young Silicon Valley talent. “The pressure is coming from, ‘I need to show off much better, quick,’” Chen continued.

Not hitting the bar has bred new anxiety. “When Zuck was building Facebook, there wasn’t this huge negative social ecosystem,” Aidan Guo, 20, told TechCrunch. He’s the co-founder of the AI desktop assistant startup Attention Engineering, which has raised around $1.6 million in funding to date.

Much of the strain, as he describes it, is self-imposed. “You already have a constant fear of failure on your mind. You have to steer the ship and learn all these things as you go. And everything can always go wrong at once,” he continued. “And then you have all these people piling on anything you do wrong. I think people need to be more empathetic.”

Amid all that pressure, Awasthi takes a page from the old days. “If you focus your time on what needs to get done, it’s not too hard,” she said.

“The best product that stays active and talks to customers wins,” Rakhmetzhanov added.

In the end, all the founders are describing the same thing: The fundamentals of a good startup haven’t changed — “conviction, intellectual honesty, and obsession with the customer,” as Smith put it. None of that has anything to do with age.

Tech.title: India is starting to pay for apps, not just download them
Tech.content:
For years, India was the world’s largest app download market but one of its toughest places to make money. That is beginning to change as Indian consumers spend more on AI, entertainment, and other premium apps.

India’s mobile app market generated a record $345 million in consumer spending during the second quarter of this year, up 35% from a year earlier, according to a new report by Sensor Tower. The app-market intelligence firm said the gains were increasingly driven by generative AI, streaming, and productivity apps rather than gaming, as Indian consumers became more willing to pay for digital subscriptions.

The record quarter builds on a broader trend of rising app monetization. India’s revenue per download has more than doubled over the past three and a half years, while quarterly app downloads have remained at around 6.3 billion since 2023.
